#385Pharmacology · post around 08:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #385!

💊 Can you name this drug class just from the ending?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Beta blockers

🧠 Rationale: Medications ending in -olol are beta blockers.

They block beta receptors, which slows the heart rate and lowers blood pressure.

ACE inhibitors end in -pril, and statins end in -statin.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Beta Blockers

💊 Examples:

🔹 Metoprolol

🔹 Atenolol

🔹 Propranolol

🔹 Carvedilol

❤️ Primary Use:

🔹 High blood pressure

🔹 Angina

🔹 Heart failure and dysrhythmias

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 Bradycardia

🔹 Low blood pressure

🔹 Fatigue and dizziness

🔹 Can hide signs of low blood sugar

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Check apical pulse and BP before giving

✅ Hold if HR under 60 or BP low and notify provider

✅ Use caution with asthma

✅ Do not stop suddenly

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

-OLOL slows the roll: slower heart, lower pressure!

📚 Want 150 more practice questions with rationales? The full question bank is linked on my profile 👤

❤️ Follow @ryan__glass for daily NCLEX practice questions!

#386Cardiac · post around 10:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #386!

❤️ Do you know the normal heart rate range by heart?

This is a HIGH-YIELD cardiac question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: D — 60 to 100/min

🧠 Rationale: A normal resting heart rate for an adult is 60 to 100 beats per minute.

Under 60 is bradycardia.

Over 100 is tachycardia.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Adult Heart Rate

❤️ Normal Range:

🔹 60 to 100 beats per minute at rest

🔹 Athletes may be lower and still healthy

⚠️ Causes of Tachycardia:

🔹 Fever and pain

🔹 Dehydration or bleeding

🔹 Anxiety

🔹 Low oxygen

⚠️ Causes of Bradycardia:

🔹 Beta blockers or digoxin

🔹 Heart block

🔹 Increased intracranial pressure

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Count for a full minute if irregular

✅ Check the client, not just the monitor

✅ Report new changes with symptoms

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

60 to 100 keeps the heart in tune!

💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #387!

🫁 This sputum color is a big clue for an emergency!

This is a HIGH-YIELD respiratory question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Pink and frothy

🧠 Rationale: Pink, frothy sputum is a classic sign of acute pulmonary edema.

Fluid backs up from the left side of the heart and leaks into the alveoli.

Rust colored sputum points to pneumococcal pneumonia.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Pulmonary Edema

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Severe shortness of breath

🔹 Crackles in the lungs

🔹 Pink, frothy sputum

🔹 Anxiety and restlessness

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Sit the client upright with legs down

✅ Give oxygen as ordered

✅ Give IV diuretics as ordered

✅ Monitor oxygen saturation and output

🚑 When to Escalate:

🔹 Falling oxygen saturation

🔹 Confusion or exhaustion

🔹 Low blood pressure

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Pink and frothy? Think fluid in the lungs, act fast!

#388Endocrine · post around 15:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #388!

🩸 Can you name the classic 3 Ps?

This is a HIGH-YIELD endocrine question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia

🧠 Rationale: High blood glucose pulls water into the urine, causing polyuria.

Fluid loss causes intense thirst, called polydipsia.

Cells cannot use glucose for energy, causing hunger, called polyphagia.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Hyperglycemia

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Polyuria: frequent urination

🔹 Polydipsia: extreme thirst

🔹 Polyphagia: extreme hunger

🔹 Blurred vision and fatigue

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Check blood glucose

✅ Give insulin or meds as ordered

✅ Encourage fluids if allowed

✅ Check for ketones in type 1 diabetes

🚑 When to Escalate:

🔹 Fruity breath or deep, rapid breathing

🔹 Confusion

🔹 Glucose very high with vomiting

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Pee, drink, eat: the 3 Ps of high sugar!

👶 Would you catch this early warning sign in a baby?

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.

✅ Correct Answer: D — Nasal flaring and chest retractions

🧠 Rationale: Nasal flaring and retractions mean the infant is working hard to breathe.

Infants mainly breathe through the nose, so flaring is an early clue.

Grunting and head bobbing are also signs of distress.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Infant Respiratory Distress

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Nasal flaring

🔹 Retractions under or between the ribs

🔹 Grunting

🔹 Head bobbing

🔹 Fast breathing

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Clear the nose with gentle suction

✅ Keep the head of bed raised

✅ Give oxygen as ordered

✅ Watch oxygen saturation

🚑 When to Escalate:

🔹 Bluish lips or skin

🔹 Pauses in breathing

🔹 Too tired to feed

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Flare and pull? Baby's working too hard!

#390Maternity · post around 19:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #390!

🤱 Prolactin or oxytocin? This one trips up so many students!

This is a HIGH-YIELD maternity question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Oxytocin

🧠 Rationale: Oxytocin causes the milk let-down (ejection) reflex.

Prolactin is the hormone that makes the milk.

Oxytocin also helps the uterus contract, which lowers bleeding after birth.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Breastfeeding Hormones

🍼 Prolactin:

🔹 Makes the milk

🔹 Rises with frequent feeding

💧 Oxytocin:

🔹 Lets the milk flow out

🔹 Helps the uterus contract

🔹 Can cause cramping during feeds

✅ Patient Teaching:

✅ Feed often, about 8 to 12 times a day

✅ Rest and drink fluids

✅ Cramping during early feeds is normal

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Prolactin PRODUCES, Oxytocin gets it OUT!

🧠 Do you know the go-to medication class for depression?

This is a HIGH-YIELD mental health question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.

.

.

✅ Correct Answer: C — SSRIs

🧠 Rationale: SSRIs are usually the first-line treatment for depression.

They have fewer serious side effects than older drugs like MAOIs.

It can take 2 to 6 weeks to feel the full effect.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: SSRIs

💊 Examples:

🔹 Sertraline

🔹 Fluoxetine

🔹 Escitalopram

🔹 Citalopram

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 Nausea and headache

🔹 Trouble sleeping

🔹 Serotonin syndrome if combined with other serotonin drugs

✅ Patient Teaching:

✅ Full effect takes several weeks

✅ Do not stop suddenly

✅ Avoid St. John's wort

✅ Report agitation, fever or tremors

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

SSRIs: Slow, Steady, Reliable, Initial choice!

#378Pharmacology · post around 08:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #378!

💓 Do you know the safe zone for this classic heart drug?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — 1.2 ng/mL

🧠 Rationale: The usual therapeutic digoxin level is about 0.5 to 2 ng/mL.

Levels above 2 ng/mL raise the risk of toxicity.

Low potassium makes toxicity more likely, even at normal levels.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Digoxin

💊 Drug Class:

🔹 Cardiac glycoside

❤️ Primary Use:

🔹 Heart failure

🔹 Atrial fibrillation rate control

⚠️ Signs of Toxicity:

🔹 Nausea, vomiting, poor appetite

🔹 Yellow or green halos in vision

🔹 Bradycardia and new dysrhythmias

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Count the apical pulse for 1 full minute

✅ Hold if adult HR is under 60 and notify provider

✅ Check potassium and digoxin levels

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Dig level 0.5 to 2: stay in the middle, watch the K!

#379Renal · post around 10:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #379!

🫘 A new kidney needs this drug for life. What matters most?

This is a HIGH-YIELD renal and pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: D — Report fever or signs of infection

🧠 Rationale: Tacrolimus suppresses the immune system to prevent rejection.

This makes infections more likely and harder to spot.

Fever can be an early sign of infection or rejection.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Tacrolimus

💊 Drug Class:

🔹 Calcineurin inhibitor (immunosuppressant)

❤️ Primary Use:

🔹 Prevent organ transplant rejection

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 Infection risk

🔹 Kidney toxicity

🔹 High potassium and high blood glucose

🔹 Tremor

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ Take at the same times every day

✅ Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice

✅ Never stop or skip doses on your own

✅ Report fever, chills, sore throat

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Immunosuppressed = infection risk. Fever is a red flag!

💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #380!

🫁 The procedure went fine, but now one finding is a big warning sign. Can you spot it?

This is a HIGH-YIELD respiratory question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.

.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Sudden dyspnea and a fast heart rate

🧠 Rationale: A thoracentesis uses a needle to drain fluid from the pleural space.

The needle can puncture the lung and cause a pneumothorax.

Sudden dyspnea and tachycardia need immediate reporting.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Thoracentesis

🩺 Before:

🔹 Verify consent

🔹 Sit upright, leaning over a bedside table

⚠️ Watch For After:

🔹 Sudden shortness of breath

🔹 Falling SpO2, fast heart rate

🔹 Decreased breath sounds on that side

🔹 Bleeding at the site

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Check vital signs and SpO2 often

✅ Listen to breath sounds

✅ Expect a chest x-ray after

✅ Apply a dressing to the site

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Needle in the chest, new dyspnea next? Think pneumothorax!

Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #381!

🦵 One number tells you a lot about blood flow to the legs. Do you know what it means?

This is a HIGH-YIELD cardiovascular question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Peripheral arterial disease

🧠 Rationale: ABI compares ankle systolic BP to arm systolic BP.

A normal ABI is about 1.0 to 1.4.

Under 0.9 suggests peripheral arterial disease. 0.6 is moderate disease.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Ankle-Brachial Index

📏 How It Works:

🔹 Ankle systolic BP divided by arm systolic BP

⚠️ PAD Signs:

🔹 Leg pain with walking (claudication)

🔹 Cool, pale legs, weak pulses

🔹 Shiny, hairless skin

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Teach walking exercise programs

✅ Teach smoking cessation

✅ Keep legs level or slightly down for comfort

✅ Report sudden pain, pallor or no pulse

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

ABI under 0.9? The arteries are in trouble!

#382GI · post around 17:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #382!

🔵 This bruise is a serious warning sign in pancreatitis. Do you know why?

This is a HIGH-YIELD GI question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Bleeding into the abdomen

🧠 Rationale: Bluish bruising around the umbilicus is Cullen sign.

In acute pancreatitis it suggests internal (retroperitoneal) bleeding.

Report it right away and watch closely for shock.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Acute Pancreatitis

⚠️ Key Signs:

🔹 Severe upper abdominal pain to the back

🔹 High serum lipase and amylase

🔹 Cullen sign: bruising around umbilicus

🔹 Grey Turner sign: bruising on the flanks

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Keep NPO to rest the pancreas

✅ Give IV fluids and pain medicine

✅ Watch BP and heart rate for shock

✅ Monitor calcium and glucose

🚑 When to Escalate:

🔹 Falling BP, rising heart rate

🔹 New bruising, confusion or low urine output

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Cullen = Center (umbilicus). Grey Turner = Turn to the flanks!

#383Peds · post around 19:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #383!

👶 Two rescuers, one tiny patient. Do you know the right ratio?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pediatric question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: D — 15 compressions to 2 breaths

🧠 Rationale: With two rescuers, infant and child CPR uses 15:2.

A single rescuer uses 30:2.

Children need more breaths because arrest is often respiratory.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Infant CPR

🫀 Compressions:

🔹 Rate 100 to 120 per minute

🔹 Depth about 1.5 inches (4 cm)

🔹 Allow full chest recoil

👐 Hand Position:

🔹 2 thumb-encircling hands technique

🔹 Heel of one hand if you cannot encircle

🚨 Key Points:

✅ Check brachial pulse

✅ Minimize pauses in compressions

✅ Switch compressor about every 2 minutes

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Two rescuers, two hands, 15:2 for little ones!

Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #384!

🦶 Normal in a baby, a red flag in an adult. Do you know this reflex?

This is a HIGH-YIELD neuro question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — An upper motor neuron problem

🧠 Rationale: The big toe going up with toes fanning is a positive Babinski sign.

In adults it suggests an upper motor neuron problem.

In infants up to about 1 to 2 years it is normal.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Babinski Reflex

🩺 How to Test:

🔹 Stroke the outer sole from heel to toes

✅ Normal Adult:

🔹 Toes curl downward (plantar flexion)

⚠️ Abnormal Adult:

🔹 Big toe up, toes fan out

🔹 Seen with stroke, spinal cord injury, MS

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Document and compare both sides

✅ Report new findings to the provider

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Babies Babinski, adults alarm!

#371Pharmacology · post around 08:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #371!

⚠️ This combo can crash a blood pressure fast. Do you know which drug it is?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Isosorbide mononitrate

🧠 Rationale: Sildenafil and nitrates both dilate blood vessels.

Together they can cause severe, life-threatening hypotension.

Nitrates like isosorbide and nitroglycerin must be avoided.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Sildenafil

💊 Drug Class:

🔹 PDE-5 inhibitor

❤️ Primary Use:

🔹 Pulmonary arterial hypertension

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 Headache and flushing

🔹 Low blood pressure

🔹 Vision changes

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Ask about all nitrate use first

✅ Check blood pressure before giving

✅ Teach to report chest pain, fainting

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Sildenafil + nitrates = BP falls off a cliff!

#372Cardiac · post around 10:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #372!

🩸 Before you stick that radial artery, there is one quick check. Do you know it?

This is a HIGH-YIELD cardiovascular question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Allen test

🧠 Rationale: The Allen test checks ulnar artery blood flow to the hand.

If the radial artery is injured, the ulnar artery must keep the hand perfused.

Color should return to the palm within about 5 to 15 seconds.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Allen Test

❤️ How To Do It:

🔹 Press on both radial and ulnar arteries

🔹 Client makes a fist, then opens a pale hand

🔹 Release the ulnar artery only

⚠️ Results:

🔹 Pink color returns fast: normal

🔹 Stays pale: do not use that radial site

🚨 After The ABG:

✅ Hold firm pressure 5 minutes or more

✅ Longer if on anticoagulants

✅ Put the sample on ice if required, send promptly

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Allen before artery: check the backup before you stick!

🫁 One shot helps protect older adults from a top cause of pneumonia. Which one?

This is a HIGH-YIELD respiratory question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

✅ Correct Answer: B — Pneumococcal vaccine

🧠 Rationale: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a leading cause of bacterial pneumonia.

Pneumococcal vaccine is recommended for older adults and high-risk clients.

The yearly flu shot also helps lower pneumonia risk.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Pneumonia Prevention

💉 Key Vaccines:

🔹 Pneumococcal vaccine

🔹 Yearly influenza vaccine

🔹 COVID-19 and RSV as recommended

⚠️ High-Risk Groups:

🔹 Older adults

🔹 Chronic heart or lung disease

🔹 Smokers and immunocompromised clients

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Check vaccine history on admission

✅ Teach hand hygiene

✅ Encourage cough and deep breathing

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Pneumo-coccal = pneumonia protection!

💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #374!

🍬 This number shows 3 months of blood sugar control. Do you know the goal?

This is a HIGH-YIELD endocrine question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

✅ Correct Answer: D — Less than 7%

🧠 Rationale: A1C reflects average blood glucose over about 2 to 3 months.

For most nonpregnant adults with diabetes, the goal is under 7%.

Goals may be looser for older adults or clients at risk for hypoglycemia.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Hemoglobin A1C

🧪 Key Numbers:

🔹 Normal: under 5.7%

🔹 Prediabetes: 5.7% to 6.4%

🔹 Diabetes: 6.5% or higher

🔹 Usual treatment goal: under 7%

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ No fasting needed for the test

✅ Checked about every 3 to 6 months

✅ Lower A1C means fewer complications

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Seven is the goal: keep A1C under 7!

Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #376!

🤱 Postpartum bleeding changes color over time. What is normal on day 2?

This is a HIGH-YIELD maternity question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Dark red flow called lochia rubra

🧠 Rationale: Lochia rubra is dark red and lasts about 1 to 3 days.

Lochia serosa is pink-brown, from about day 4 to 10.

Lochia alba is white or yellow and can last up to 6 weeks.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Lochia Stages

🔴 Rubra:

🔹 Dark red, days 1 to 3

🩷 Serosa:

🔹 Pink-brown, days 4 to 10

⚪ Alba:

🔹 White or yellow, up to 6 weeks

🚨 When To Escalate:

✅ Soaking a pad in 1 hour

✅ Large clots

✅ Foul odor or fever

✅ Bright red flow returns after it lightened

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Red, pink, white: rubra, serosa, alba!

💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #377!

🧠 Positive vs negative symptoms trip up so many students. Can you pick the negative one?

This is a HIGH-YIELD mental health question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Flat affect

🧠 Rationale: Negative symptoms are a loss of normal function.

Flat affect means little or no facial expression or emotion.

Hallucinations, delusions and disorganized speech are positive symptoms.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Schizophrenia Symptoms

➕ Positive (added):

🔹 Hallucinations

🔹 Delusions

🔹 Disorganized speech or behavior

➖ Negative (missing):

🔹 Flat affect

🔹 Lack of motivation (avolition)

🔹 Little speech (alogia)

🔹 Social withdrawal

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Build trust with short, frequent contact

✅ Encourage self-care in small steps

✅ Give meds as ordered, watch side effects

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Negative = something is missing!

#364Pharmacology · post around 08:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #364!

🔥 This antifungal is famous for a nickname nursing students never forget. Do you know why?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Fever, chills and shaking

🧠 Rationale: Amphotericin B often causes infusion reactions within the first hours.

Fever, chills and rigors are the classic signs.

Premedication and a slow infusion help prevent them.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Amphotericin B

💊 Drug Class:

🔹 Antifungal (polyene)

❤️ Primary Use:

🔹 Serious systemic fungal infections

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 Fever, chills, rigors

🔹 Kidney damage (nephrotoxicity)

🔹 Low potassium and magnesium

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Premedicate as ordered (acetaminophen, diphenhydramine)

✅ Monitor kidney function and electrolytes

✅ Infuse slowly, check vitals often

✅ Watch intake and output

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Amphotericin B = "shake and bake" (chills and fever)!

#365Cardiac · post around 10:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #365!

👂 Lub-dub-DUB. That extra sound could mean trouble. Do you know what it means?

This is a HIGH-YIELD cardiac question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Fluid overload or heart failure

🧠 Rationale: An S3 happens when blood rushes into a stiff or overfilled ventricle.

In older adults it usually signals heart failure or fluid overload.

It can be normal in children, young adults and pregnancy.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: S3 Heart Sound

❤️ What It Is:

🔹 Extra sound right after S2

🔹 Sounds like "Ken-tuc-ky"

🔹 Also called a ventricular gallop

⚠️ Linked To:

🔹 Heart failure

🔹 Fluid volume overload

🔹 Mitral regurgitation

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Listen at the apex with the bell

✅ Check lung sounds for crackles

✅ Check daily weight and edema

✅ Report new S3 to the provider

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

S3 = "Ken-tuc-ky" = too much fluid in the tank!

#366Respiratory · post around 12:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #366!

🫁 Fluid around the lung changes everything you hear. Can you pick the right finding?

This is a HIGH-YIELD respiratory question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: D — Dullness and decreased breath sounds

🧠 Rationale: Fluid in the pleural space muffles sound and blocks airflow.

Percussion is dull and breath sounds are decreased or absent.

Hyperresonance points to air, as in a pneumothorax.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Pleural Effusion

🫁 What It Is:

🔹 Extra fluid between lung and chest wall

❤️ Common Causes:

🔹 Heart failure

🔹 Pneumonia

🔹 Cancer

🔹 Kidney or liver disease

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Shortness of breath

🔹 Dull percussion

🔹 Decreased breath sounds and fremitus

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Raise the head of the bed

✅ Give oxygen as ordered

✅ Prepare for thoracentesis

✅ Monitor SpO2 and breathing

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Fluid = Flat and dull. Air = hyper and loud!

#367Endocrine · post around 15:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #367!

💉 Not all injection sites work at the same speed. Which one wins the race?

This is a HIGH-YIELD endocrine question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Abdomen

🧠 Rationale: The abdomen absorbs subcutaneous insulin the fastest.

The arm is next, then the thigh and buttock.

Rotating within one area keeps absorption more predictable.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Insulin Injection Sites

💉 Absorption Order:

🔹 Abdomen (fastest)

🔹 Upper arm

🔹 Thigh

🔹 Buttock (slowest)

⚠️ Problems to Avoid:

🔹 Lipohypertrophy from same-spot injections

🔹 Injecting into scars or bruises

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ Rotate sites within one area

✅ Stay 2 inches away from the navel

✅ Check glucose as instructed

✅ Exercise can speed absorption from a limb

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

A is for Abdomen and A is for Absorbs fastest!

💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #368!

🦷 This antibiotic can leave a lasting mark on a child's smile. Do you know why?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pediatric pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Permanent tooth staining

🧠 Rationale: Tetracyclines bind to calcium in developing teeth and bones.

This can cause permanent yellow or brown tooth staining.

Doxycycline may still be used short term for some serious infections.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Tetracyclines in Children

💊 Drug Class:

🔹 Tetracyclines (tetracycline, doxycycline, minocycline)

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 Tooth staining in young children

🔹 Sun sensitivity

🔹 GI upset

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ Avoid in pregnancy and under age 8 unless prescribed

✅ Do not take with milk, antacids or iron

✅ Use sunscreen and limit sun

✅ Take with a full glass of water

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Tetracycline + Tots = Tinted Teeth!

#369Maternity · post around 19:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #369!

⏱️ Timing contractions sounds easy, but many students mix this up. Do you know the rule?

This is a HIGH-YIELD maternity question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — From the start of one to the start of the next

🧠 Rationale: Frequency is timed from the start of one contraction to the start of the next.

Duration is timed from the start to the end of one contraction.

Contractions closer than every 2 minutes need follow-up.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Timing Contractions

⏱️ Key Terms:

🔹 Frequency: start to start

🔹 Duration: start to end

🔹 Intensity: strength at the peak

⚠️ Report Right Away:

🔹 Contractions more often than every 2 minutes

🔹 Contractions lasting over 90 seconds

🔹 No rest between contractions

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Palpate the fundus or use the monitor

✅ Check fetal heart rate with contractions

✅ Stop oxytocin if contractions are too frequent

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Frequency = Start to Start. Duration = Start to Stop!

#370Mental Health · post around 21:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #370!

🗣️ Therapeutic communication shows up everywhere on the NCLEX. Can you spot the right technique?

This is a HIGH-YIELD mental health question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — "You're worried about going home?"

🧠 Rationale: Reflection repeats the client's feelings back so the client can explore them.

False reassurance and changing the subject shut down talking.

"Why" questions can make clients feel defensive.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Therapeutic Communication

✅ Therapeutic Techniques:

🔹 Reflection: repeat feelings back

🔹 Open-ended questions

🔹 Active listening and silence

🔹 Clarifying

⚠️ Nontherapeutic Responses:

🔹 False reassurance

🔹 "Why" questions

🔹 Changing the subject

🔹 Giving advice

🚨 NCLEX Strategy:

✅ Pick the answer that focuses on feelings

✅ Keep the focus on the client

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Reflect it back like a mirror: feelings first!

#357Pharmacology · post around 08:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #357!

🍌 Potassium pills can hurt the stomach if taken the wrong way. Do you know the rule?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Swallow it whole with food and plenty of water

🧠 Rationale: Oral potassium irritates the stomach and esophagus.

Crushing an extended-release tablet releases the whole dose at once.

Salt substitutes contain potassium and can push levels too high.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Potassium Chloride (Oral)

💊 Drug Class:

🔹 Electrolyte replacement

❤️ Primary Use:

🔹 Low potassium (hypokalemia)

🔹 Often given with loop or thiazide diuretics

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 Nausea, stomach upset

🔹 GI irritation or ulcers

🔹 High potassium if overdosed

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Check potassium and kidney function

✅ Give with food and a full glass of water

✅ Do not crush extended-release tablets

✅ Teach to avoid salt substitutes unless approved

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Potassium pill? Whole, with food, with water!

#358Cardiac · post around 10:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #358!

🫀 Lub-dub! Do you know which valves make the dub?

This is a HIGH-YIELD cardiac question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Closing of the aortic and pulmonic valves

🧠 Rationale: S2 (dub) happens when the aortic and pulmonic valves close.

It marks the end of systole and the start of diastole.

S1 (lub) is closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Heart Sounds

❤️ S1 (Lub):

🔹 Mitral and tricuspid valves close

🔹 Start of systole

🔹 Loudest at the apex

❤️ S2 (Dub):

🔹 Aortic and pulmonic valves close

🔹 Start of diastole

🔹 Loudest at the base

⚠️ Extra Sounds:

🔹 S3: may mean heart failure

🔹 S4: stiff ventricle, like long-term high BP

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Listen with the diaphragm for S1 and S2

✅ Report new extra sounds or murmurs

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

S1 = AV valves shut. S2 = Semilunar valves shut. 1 before 2, A before S!

#359Endocrine · post around 12:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #359!

💉 Only one of these insulins belongs in an IV bag. Which one?

This is a HIGH-YIELD endocrine question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: D — Regular insulin

🧠 Rationale: Regular insulin is the standard insulin for IV infusions in DKA.

NPH is cloudy and is never given IV.

Glargine and detemir are long-acting and given subcut only.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Insulin Types

⚡ Rapid-Acting:

🔹 Lispro, aspart, glulisine

🔹 Give with meals

💧 Short-Acting:

🔹 Regular insulin

🔹 Clear, the main insulin used IV

☁️ Intermediate:

🔹 NPH, cloudy

🔹 Subcut only

🕐 Long-Acting:

🔹 Glargine, detemir, degludec

🔹 Steady basal coverage, do not mix

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Check potassium before starting the drip

✅ Check glucose every hour on an infusion

✅ Use an infusion pump

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Regular rides the IV road!

#360Peds · post around 15:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #360!

🦶 A newborn's foot turns in and down. What is the first step to fix it?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pediatric question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Serial casting soon after birth

🧠 Rationale: Treatment starts early, often in the first 1 to 2 weeks.

Casts are changed about weekly to slowly correct the foot.

A brace is then worn for several years to prevent relapse.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Clubfoot (Talipes Equinovarus)

👶 What It Is:

🔹 Foot turned inward and downward

🔹 Can affect one or both feet

🩹 Treatment:

🔹 Serial casting (Ponseti method)

🔹 Often a small heel cord release

🔹 Foot abduction brace afterward

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Check toes for color, warmth and movement

✅ Keep the cast clean and dry

✅ Report swelling or cool, pale toes

✅ Teach parents brace routine

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Clubfoot? Cast early, cast often, then brace!

#361Maternity · post around 17:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #361!

🤰 This is more than normal morning sickness. Can you name it?

This is a HIGH-YIELD maternity question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Hyperemesis gravidarum

🧠 Rationale: Normal morning sickness does not cause weight loss or ketones.

Hyperemesis causes dehydration and electrolyte problems.

Preeclampsia and gestational diabetes usually appear after 20 weeks.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Hyperemesis Gravidarum

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Vomiting many times a day

🔹 Weight loss of 5% or more

🔹 Ketones in urine, dehydration

🩸 Labs to Watch:

🔹 Potassium and sodium

🔹 Urine specific gravity

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ IV fluids and antiemetics as ordered

✅ Daily weights, intake and output

✅ Small, frequent bland meals once tolerated

✅ Offer emotional support

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Hyperemesis = hyper vomiting + weight loss + ketones!

#362Mental Health · post around 19:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #362!

🏋️ Turning anger into gym time. Which defense mechanism is it?

This is a HIGH-YIELD mental health question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Sublimation

🧠 Rationale: Sublimation turns strong feelings into a positive, accepted activity.

Displacement would be taking the anger out on a safer target.

Sublimation is considered a healthy, mature defense.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Defense Mechanisms

🧠 Common Ones:

🔹 Sublimation: feelings into healthy activity

🔹 Displacement: feelings onto a safer target

🔹 Projection: blaming others for your own feelings

🔹 Repression: unconsciously blocking memories

✅ Healthy vs Unhealthy:

🔹 Sublimation and humor are mature

🔹 Denial and projection can block coping

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Notice the behavior without judging

✅ Encourage healthy coping skills

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Sublimation = Sweat it out in a Socially accepted way!

#363Neuro · post around 21:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #363!

👁️ One pupil just blew after a head injury. What does it mean?

This is a HIGH-YIELD neuro question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: D — Rising ICP pressing on cranial nerve III

🧠 Rationale: Rising pressure in the skull can press on cranial nerve III.

This makes the pupil on that side fixed and dilated.

Opioids cause small (pinpoint) pupils, not dilated ones.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Pupils and Increased ICP

⚠️ Signs of Rising ICP:

🔹 Change in LOC (earliest sign)

🔹 Fixed, dilated pupil (late sign)

🔹 Cushing triad: high SBP, low HR, irregular breathing

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Notify the provider right away

✅ Head of bed 30 degrees, head midline

✅ Frequent neuro checks

✅ Avoid coughing, straining and hip flexion

🚑 Emergency:

🔹 A blown pupil can mean brain herniation

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Blown pupil = brain pressure. Call it in NOW!

#350Pharmacology · post around 08:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #350!

👂 Ringing ears on a daily pain reliever? Know this warning sign!

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Salicylate (aspirin) toxicity

🧠 Rationale: Tinnitus is a classic early sign of salicylate toxicity.

Hold the dose and report it to the provider.

Other signs include nausea, fast breathing and confusion.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Aspirin (Salicylates)

💊 Drug Class:

🔹 NSAID, salicylate, antiplatelet

❤️ Primary Use:

🔹 Pain, fever, inflammation

🔹 Low dose to prevent heart attack and stroke

⚠️ Toxicity Signs:

🔹 Tinnitus or hearing loss

🔹 Nausea, vomiting

🔹 Rapid breathing, confusion

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Hold the dose and notify the provider

✅ Teach to take with food

✅ Watch for GI bleeding

✅ Avoid in children with viral illness (Reye syndrome)

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Aspirin overload rings the alarm: tinnitus = toxicity!

#351Cardiac · post around 10:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #351!

❤️ Going home with a heart monitor? What is the client's job?

This is a HIGH-YIELD cardiac question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: D — Keep a diary of activities and symptoms

🧠 Rationale: A Holter monitor records the heart rhythm for 24 to 48 hours.

The diary lets the provider match symptoms to the rhythm.

The client should do normal daily activities and keep the device dry.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Holter Monitor

❤️ Purpose:

🔹 Records continuous ECG at home

🔹 Finds rhythm problems that come and go

📝 Patient Teaching:

✅ Write down activities, symptoms and times

✅ Keep up normal daily activities

✅ Do not shower or swim while wearing it

✅ Keep electrodes on the skin

⚠️ Report Right Away:

🔹 Chest pain, fainting or severe dizziness

🔹 Call 911 for emergencies, do not wait for results

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Holter = Hold on and write it down. Live normally, log every symptom!

#352Respiratory · post around 12:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #352!

🫁 Day 1 after surgery, quiet lung bases and a low fever. What helps most?

This is a HIGH-YIELD respiratory question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Cough, deep breathe and use the spirometer

🧠 Rationale: These findings point to atelectasis, collapsed alveoli.

Coughing, deep breathing and the incentive spirometer reopen the alveoli.

Good pain control helps the client breathe deeply.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Postoperative Atelectasis

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Diminished breath sounds at the bases

🔹 Low-grade fever in the first day or two

🔹 Low SpO2, shortness of breath

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Incentive spirometer 10 times every hour while awake

✅ Turn, cough and deep breathe

✅ Get the client up and walking early

✅ Splint the incision with a pillow

✅ Give pain medication as ordered

🚑 When to Escalate:

🔹 SpO2 keeps dropping

🔹 Fever rises or sputum changes

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Atelectasis after surgery? Breathe deep, cough strong, walk long!

#353Endocrine · post around 15:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #353!

👁️ Bulging eyes from an overactive thyroid. How do you protect them?

This is a HIGH-YIELD endocrine question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Use eye drops and raise the head of the bed

🧠 Rationale: Exophthalmos can keep the eyelids from closing fully.

Artificial tears keep the cornea moist.

Raising the head of the bed reduces swelling around the eyes.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Exophthalmos (Graves Disease)

⚠️ Signs of Graves Disease:

🔹 Bulging eyes

🔹 Weight loss, heat intolerance

🔹 Fast heart rate, tremor

🚨 Eye Care Teaching:

✅ Use artificial tears often

✅ Raise the head of the bed at night

✅ Wear dark glasses outside

✅ Tape eyelids closed at night if ordered

✅ Limit salt to reduce swelling

🚑 Report Right Away:

🔹 Eye pain or vision changes

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Graves eyes: Moisten, Elevate, Shield!

This is a HIGH-YIELD pediatric question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: D — Pulls to stand and cruises furniture

🧠 Rationale: Most 12-month-olds pull to stand and walk while holding furniture.

Many take first steps alone around this age.

Running and kicking a ball come closer to age 2, and a tricycle around age 3.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: 12-Month Milestones

🧸 Motor Skills:

🔹 Pulls to stand, cruises furniture

🔹 May take first steps alone

🔹 Pincer grasp to pick up small things

🗣️ Language + Social:

🔹 Says mama or dada and 1 to 2 words

🔹 Waves bye-bye

🔹 Plays simple games like peekaboo

📏 Growth:

🔹 Birth weight about triples by 1 year

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Refer if the child cannot stand with support

✅ Refer if the child loses skills

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

At 1 year: Stand, cruise, wave and say a word!

#355Maternity · post around 19:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #355!

🤰 A drug to slow early labor. Which side effect do you watch for?

This is a HIGH-YIELD maternity question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Fast heart rate (tachycardia)

🧠 Rationale: Terbutaline is a beta-2 agonist that relaxes the uterus.

It stimulates the heart and causes tachycardia and tremors.

Hold it and notify the provider if the maternal heart rate is over 120/min.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Terbutaline (Tocolytic)

💊 Drug Class:

🔹 Beta-2 adrenergic agonist

❤️ Primary Use:

🔹 Short-term delay of preterm labor

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 Maternal and fetal tachycardia

🔹 Tremors, nervousness

🔹 High blood glucose, low potassium

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Check maternal HR before each dose

✅ Monitor fetal heart rate

✅ Report chest pain or shortness of breath

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Terbutaline = Tachycardia. Both start with T!

Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #356!

🧠 The client does not want to talk. What should the nurse say?

This is a HIGH-YIELD mental health question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — I will sit here with you for a while.

🧠 Rationale: Offering self shows caring and respect without pushing.

"Why" questions can make a client defensive.

Giving advice or leaving for a full day blocks trust.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Therapeutic Communication

✅ Therapeutic Techniques:

🔹 Offering self

🔹 Silence

🔹 Open-ended questions

🔹 Reflecting feelings

⚠️ Nontherapeutic Blocks:

🔹 Asking why

🔹 Giving advice or false reassurance

🔹 Changing the subject

🔹 Leaving the client alone for long periods

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Respect the client's pace

✅ Stay calm and present

✅ Check back often

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

When they won't talk, don't walk. Offer yourself!

#343Pharmacology · post around 08:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #343!

💉 This injection technique keeps iron from staining the skin!

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Use the Z-track method

🧠 Rationale: Iron dextran can stain the skin and irritate tissue.

The Z-track method seals the medication deep in the muscle.

Do not massage the site, because that pushes iron back into the tissue.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Iron Dextran (IM)

💊 Drug Class:

🔹 Parenteral iron replacement

❤️ Primary Use:

🔹 Iron deficiency anemia when oral iron fails

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 Skin staining at the site

🔹 Joint aches, fever

🔹 Anaphylaxis (rare but serious)

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Use a large deep muscle like the ventrogluteal

✅ Change the needle after drawing it up

✅ Use Z-track, do not massage

✅ Give a test dose if ordered and watch closely

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Z-track = Zero leak. Pull the skin, inject, wait, release!

#344Cardiac · post around 10:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #344!

❤️ Three symptoms that point straight to a tight heart valve!

This is a HIGH-YIELD cardiac question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: D — Chest pain, fainting and breathlessness with exertion

🧠 Rationale: A narrowed aortic valve limits blood flow out of the heart.

During exertion the heart cannot raise its output enough.

This causes angina, syncope and heart failure symptoms.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Aortic Stenosis

❤️ What Happens:

🔹 The aortic valve narrows and stiffens

🔹 The left ventricle works harder and thickens

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Angina

🔹 Syncope

🔹 Dyspnea on exertion

🔹 Harsh systolic murmur at the right second intercostal space

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Teach the client to avoid heavy exertion

✅ Rise slowly, watch for fainting

✅ Monitor for heart failure signs

🚑 When to escalate:

🔹 New fainting, chest pain or worsening shortness of breath

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Aortic stenosis = SAD: Syncope, Angina, Dyspnea!

#345GI · post around 12:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #345!

🍽️ No stomach means one vitamin can no longer be absorbed!

This is a HIGH-YIELD GI question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Vitamin B12 injections

🧠 Rationale: The stomach makes intrinsic factor.

Without intrinsic factor, vitamin B12 cannot be absorbed from food.

Lifelong B12 shots or nasal spray prevent pernicious anemia.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Total Gastrectomy

🔬 Why B12:

🔹 The stomach's parietal cells make intrinsic factor

🔹 Intrinsic factor is needed to absorb B12

⚠️ Signs of B12 Deficiency:

🔹 Fatigue and pallor

🔹 Smooth, red tongue

🔹 Numbness and tingling in hands and feet

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ Get B12 injections for life

✅ Eat small, frequent meals

✅ Watch for dumping syndrome

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

No stomach, no intrinsic factor, no B12. Give the shot!

💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #346!

🕊️ One sentence tells you exactly which stage of grief this is!

This is a HIGH-YIELD mental health question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Bargaining

🧠 Rationale: Bargaining is trying to make a deal for more time.

It often uses "if" or "just let me" statements.

The nurse listens and supports the client without false hope.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Stages of Grief (Kubler-Ross)

🧠 The 5 Stages:

🔹 Denial: "This can't be happening"

🔹 Anger: "Why me?"

🔹 Bargaining: "If I can just..."

🔹 Depression: deep sadness, withdrawal

🔹 Acceptance: "I'm ready"

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Listen actively and stay present

✅ Allow the client to express feelings

✅ Avoid false reassurance

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Bargaining sounds like a deal: "If... then..."

#347Safety · post around 17:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #347!

🔥 Hot, dry and confused after a run? Every second counts!

This is a HIGH-YIELD emergency care question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Begin rapid cooling

🧠 Rationale: These are signs of heat stroke, a medical emergency.

Rapid cooling, like cold water immersion or ice packs, saves brain and organs.

Antipyretics do not work for heat stroke, and a confused client should not drink.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Heat Stroke

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Core temp 104°F (40°C) or higher

🔹 Confusion or seizures

🔹 Hot skin, may be dry

🔹 Fast heart rate

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Call for help and start cooling now

✅ Cold water immersion or ice packs to neck, armpits, groin

✅ Give IV fluids as ordered

✅ Stop cooling at about 102°F (39°C) to avoid shivering

🚑 Emergency:

🔹 Heat stroke can cause organ failure and death

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Heat stroke: cool first, transport second!

#348Peds · post around 19:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #348!

🧸 A toddler can't tell you a number, so how do you measure pain?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pediatric question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: D — FLACC scale

🧠 Rationale: A 2-year-old cannot reliably self-report pain.

FLACC uses behavior: Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability.

FACES is used starting around age 3, and numeric scales for older children.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Pediatric Pain Scales

📏 Which Scale When:

🔹 FLACC: infants to about age 3 or nonverbal

🔹 Wong-Baker FACES: about age 3 and up

🔹 Numeric 0 to 10: about age 8 and up

⚠️ FLACC Scores:

🔹 Each category 0 to 2

🔹 Total 0 to 10

🔹 Higher score = more pain

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Reassess pain after every intervention

✅ Involve parents in comfort care

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

FLACC = Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability!

#349Safety · post around 21:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #349!

📝 Where does the incident report go? Most students miss this one!

This is a HIGH-YIELD safety and legal question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Do not mention the incident report in the chart

🧠 Rationale: An incident report is an internal quality tool, not part of the medical record.

Chart only the facts of the fall, the assessment and the care given.

Mentioning the report in the chart can make it part of the legal record.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Incident Reports

📋 Purpose:

🔹 Track errors and safety events

🔹 Improve care, not punish staff

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Assess the client first

✅ Notify the provider

✅ Chart objective facts only

✅ File the report, but never reference it in the chart

⚠️ Never:

🔹 Copy it into the chart

🔹 Blame others in writing

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Chart the fall, not the form!

#336Pharmacology · post around 08:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #336!

💉 One question before that first antibiotic dose could prevent a code!

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Penicillin allergy

🧠 Rationale: Ceftriaxone is a cephalosporin.

Cephalosporins and penicillins share a beta-lactam ring.

A history of severe penicillin reaction raises the risk of anaphylaxis.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Cephalosporins

💊 Drug Class:

🔹 Cephalosporin antibiotic (third generation)

❤️ Primary Use:

🔹 Pneumonia, meningitis, serious infections

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 Rash, diarrhea

🔹 C. diff infection

🔹 Anaphylaxis (rare but deadly)

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Ask about allergies before the first dose

✅ Get cultures before starting if ordered

✅ Watch closely during the first infusion

🚑 When to escalate:

🔹 Hives, wheezing, throat tightness or low BP

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

CEF and PEN are cousins. Ask about one before giving the other!

#337Endocrine · post around 10:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #337!

🧠 The surgeon went in through the nose. What should the client avoid now?

This is a HIGH-YIELD endocrine question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: D — Avoid coughing, sneezing hard or blowing the nose

🧠 Rationale: The surgery goes through the nose and sphenoid sinus.

Coughing, sneezing, nose blowing and bending raise pressure at the site.

This can cause a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Transsphenoidal Hypophysectomy

⚠️ Watch For:

🔹 Clear nasal drainage (possible CSF leak)

🔹 Headache that gets worse

🔹 Large urine output (diabetes insipidus)

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Keep head of bed raised

✅ Test clear drainage for glucose and report it

✅ Track intake, output and urine specific gravity

✅ No toothbrushing until cleared, use mouth rinses

🚑 When to escalate:

🔹 Clear drainage, stiff neck or fever

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Through the NOSE? Don't BLOW it!

Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #338!

👶 Grab your scorecard. Can you add up this newborn's Apgar?

This is a HIGH-YIELD maternity question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — 8

🧠 Rationale: Heart rate over 100 = 2, strong cry = 2, active motion = 2.

Grimace = 1 and blue hands and feet = 1.

Total score = 8, a normal result.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Apgar Score

📋 Checked At:

🔹 1 minute and 5 minutes after birth

🔹 5 signs, 0 to 2 points each

🔹 Heart rate, breathing, tone, reflexes, color

✅ Score Meaning:

🔹 7 to 10: normal

🔹 4 to 6: needs some help

🔹 0 to 3: needs immediate resuscitation

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Dry and warm the newborn

✅ Blue hands and feet are common at first (acrocyanosis)

🚑 When to escalate:

🔹 Heart rate under 100 or weak breathing

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

APGAR = Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration!

#339Cardiac · post around 15:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #339!

❤️ The atria and ventricles are not talking to each other. Name this rhythm!

This is a HIGH-YIELD cardiac question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Third-degree (complete) heart block

🧠 Rationale: In third-degree block, no impulses reach the ventricles.

The atria and ventricles beat on their own.

The heart rate is often very slow.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Third-Degree Heart Block

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Slow heart rate, often under 40/min

🔹 Dizziness or fainting

🔹 Low blood pressure, fatigue

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Assess the client first

✅ Prepare for transcutaneous pacing if unstable

✅ Expect a permanent pacemaker

🚑 When to escalate:

🔹 Low BP, chest pain or confusion

📈 Quick Rhythm Review:

🔹 First-degree: long PR interval

🔹 Type I: PR gets longer until a QRS drops

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

3rd degree = the P's and Q's are DIVORCED!

💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #340!

🧩 A new admission, a new place. What helps this child feel safe?

This is a HIGH-YIELD mental health question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: D — Keep a consistent daily routine

🧠 Rationale: Children with autism cope best with routine and predictability.

Consistent staff and a quiet room lower distress.

Unexpected touch and noise can overwhelm the child.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Autism Spectrum Disorder

⚠️ Common Signs:

🔹 Trouble with social communication

🔹 Repetitive behaviors

🔹 Sensitivity to sound, light or touch

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Keep routines like home as much as possible

✅ Assign the same caregivers

✅ Use a quiet, low-stimulation room

✅ Ask parents what calms the child

🚑 When to escalate:

🔹 Self-injury risk or severe distress

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Same nurse, same routine, same calm!

Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #341!

🩸 This post-op pain med is strong, but one finding means stop!

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Black, tarry stools

🧠 Rationale: Ketorolac is a strong NSAID.

It can cause GI bleeding and kidney injury.

Black, tarry stools suggest an upper GI bleed.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Ketorolac (Toradol)

💊 Drug Class:

🔹 NSAID

❤️ Primary Use:

🔹 Short-term moderate to severe pain

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 GI bleeding

🔹 Kidney injury

🔹 Bleeding risk

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Limit use to 5 days total

✅ Monitor urine output and kidney labs

✅ Ask about ulcers and bleeding history

🚑 When to escalate:

🔹 Black stools, vomiting blood or low urine output

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

KetoroLAC: LACks stomach protection. 5 days max!

#342Legal + Ethics · post around 21:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #342!

🔒 Privacy matters! Which nurse is doing it right?

This is a HIGH-YIELD legal and ethics question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Logging off the computer before walking away

🧠 Rationale: Logging off prevents others from viewing health records.

Public places like elevators are never safe for client talk.

Photos and phone calls can easily leak private details.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: HIPAA and Confidentiality

🔐 Protect Privacy:

🔹 Log off every time you step away

🔹 Talk about clients only in private areas

🔹 Share details only with the care team

📱 Social Media:

🔹 No client photos or details, ever

🔹 Even without names, it can still be a violation

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Verify who is calling before sharing anything

✅ Follow the client's privacy wishes

🚑 When to escalate:

🔹 Report any privacy breach to your manager

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

If it's not your client, it's not your business!

#329Pharmacology · post around 08:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #329!

🔥 The temperature is climbing fast in the OR. What do you grab?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Dantrolene

🧠 Rationale: These are signs of malignant hyperthermia.

Dantrolene relaxes the muscles and stops the runaway heat.

Succinylcholine can trigger it, so it must be stopped.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Malignant Hyperthermia

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Rising end-tidal CO2 (often first)

🔹 Muscle rigidity, jaw tightness

🔹 Fast heart rate, high fever

💊 Triggers:

🔹 Inhaled anesthetic gases

🔹 Succinylcholine

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Stop the trigger agent

✅ Give dantrolene IV

✅ Cool the client, give 100% oxygen

🚑 When to escalate:

🔹 Any unexplained rise in CO2 or temperature during anesthesia

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

DANTROLENE puts out the fire!

Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #330!

👀 This TB drug can affect one sense. Do you know which?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Blurred vision or trouble seeing red and green

🧠 Rationale: Ethambutol can damage the optic nerve.

Early signs are blurry vision and trouble telling red from green.

Orange urine is expected with rifampin, not ethambutol.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Ethambutol

💊 Drug Class:

🔹 First-line TB medication

❤️ Primary Use:

🔹 Active tuberculosis, with other TB drugs

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 Optic neuritis

🔹 Red-green color changes

🔹 Raised uric acid

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Check vision before starting

✅ Repeat eye checks during therapy

✅ Teach to report vision changes fast

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

E for Ethambutol, E for EYES!

#331Maternity · post around 12:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #331!

🚨 Early pregnancy, one-sided pain and shoulder pain. What is going on?

This is a HIGH-YIELD maternity question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Ruptured ectopic pregnancy

🧠 Rationale: One-sided pain early in pregnancy is a warning sign of ectopic pregnancy.

Shoulder pain suggests bleeding inside the abdomen that irritates the diaphragm.

This is an emergency.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Ectopic Pregnancy

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Sharp one-sided pelvic pain

🔹 Shoulder pain from internal bleeding

🔹 Dizziness, low BP, fast pulse

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Check vital signs often

✅ Start IV access, keep NPO

✅ Prepare for surgery or methotrexate

🚑 When to escalate:

🔹 Signs of shock: report right away

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Early pregnancy + shoulder pain = think rupture!

#332Renal · post around 15:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #332!

🧠 First dialysis session and the client feels awful. Why?

This is a HIGH-YIELD renal question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: D — Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome

🧠 Rationale: Urea is removed from the blood faster than from the brain.

Fluid shifts into brain cells and causes swelling.

It is most common during the first sessions.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Dialysis Disequilibrium Syndrome

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Headache, nausea, vomiting

🔹 Restlessness, confusion

🔹 Seizures if severe

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Slow the dialysis rate

✅ Report to the provider

✅ Use shorter first sessions

🚑 When to escalate:

🔹 Confusion or seizure activity

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Too FAST a pull = brain SWELL!

Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #333!

👶 Fever spike and a seizure. What should the parents do?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pediatrics question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Lay the child on the side, time it

🧠 Rationale: Side-lying keeps the airway open and lets saliva drain.

Timing the seizure helps the provider decide care.

Never put anything in the mouth or hold the child down.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Febrile Seizures

❤️ Who gets them:

🔹 Children 6 months to 5 years

🔹 Often with a fast rising fever

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ Stay calm, place child on the side

✅ Move objects away

✅ Time the seizure

🚑 When to escalate:

🔹 Call 911 if it lasts over 5 minutes

🔹 Trouble breathing or blue color

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

SIDE, SAFE, TIME it!

✅ Correct Answer: B — Involuntary movements of the face or tongue

🧠 Rationale: Metoclopramide can cause tardive dyskinesia.

Signs include lip smacking and tongue movements.

It can be permanent, so stop the drug and report it.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Metoclopramide (Reglan)

💊 Drug Class:

🔹 Antiemetic, GI motility drug

❤️ Primary Use:

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 Tardive dyskinesia

🔹 Restlessness, drowsiness

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Give 30 minutes before meals

✅ Watch for abnormal movements

✅ Limit use to 12 weeks

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

REGLAN can make you WIGGLE: watch for movements!

#322Pharmacology · post around 08:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #322!

💧 It pulls off fluid fast, but what else does it pull out?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Potassium

🧠 Rationale: Furosemide is a loop diuretic that makes the kidneys flush out water and sodium.

Potassium is lost too.

Low potassium can cause muscle weakness and dangerous heart rhythms.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Furosemide (Lasix)

💊 Drug Class:

🔹 Loop diuretic

❤️ Primary Use:

🔹 Heart failure

🔹 Edema

🔹 High blood pressure

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 Low potassium

🔹 Dehydration and low BP

🔹 Ringing in the ears with fast IV push

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Check potassium before giving

✅ Weigh daily, track I and O

✅ Give early in the day to avoid night urination

🚑 When to escalate:

🔹 K+ under 3.5 mEq/L

🔹 Muscle cramps, weakness or irregular pulse

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

LOOP diuretics make you LOSE potassium!

❤️ Not every heart attack looks like the movies!

This is a HIGH-YIELD cardiac question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Fatigue, nausea, and jaw or back pain

🧠 Rationale: Women are more likely to have subtle heart attack symptoms.

These include fatigue, nausea, shortness of breath and jaw, neck or back pain.

These signs are often missed, which delays treatment.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: MI in Women

⚠️ Common Signs in Women:

🔹 Unusual fatigue

🔹 Nausea or indigestion

🔹 Shortness of breath

🔹 Jaw, neck or back pain

❤️ Classic Signs:

🔹 Chest pressure or tightness

🔹 Pain spreading to the left arm

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Get a 12-lead ECG fast

✅ Check troponin

✅ Never ignore vague symptoms

🚑 Emergency:

🔹 Call 911 for any possible MI symptoms

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Women whisper, men shout: listen for the quiet signs!

#324Respiratory · post around 12:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #324!

🫁 ABGs scare everyone. Can you spot the normal one?

This is a HIGH-YIELD respiratory question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: D — 40 mmHg

🧠 Rationale: Normal PaCO2 is 35 to 45 mmHg.

40 mmHg is right in the middle of the normal range.

PaCO2 is the respiratory part of the ABG.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: ABG Normal Values

🧪 Normal Ranges:

🔹 pH: 7.35 to 7.45

🔹 PaCO2: 35 to 45 mmHg

🔹 HCO3: 22 to 26 mEq/L

🔹 PaO2: 80 to 100 mmHg

⚠️ PaCO2 Changes:

🔹 Above 45: respiratory acidosis (hypoventilation)

🔹 Below 35: respiratory alkalosis (hyperventilation)

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Check pH first

✅ Then match PaCO2 or HCO3 to the pH

✅ Treat the client, not just the numbers

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

CO2 is an ACID: more CO2 means more acid!

Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #325!

💉 Four insulins, only one works fast. Which one?

This is a HIGH-YIELD endocrine question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Insulin lispro

🧠 Rationale: Insulin lispro is rapid-acting.

It starts working in about 15 minutes, so it is given with meals.

Glargine and detemir are long-acting. NPH is intermediate-acting.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Insulin Types

⚡ Rapid-Acting:

🔹 Lispro, aspart, glulisine

🔹 Onset about 15 minutes

🔹 Give with meals

⏱️ Short-Acting:

🔹 Regular insulin

🔹 Onset 30 to 60 minutes

🔹 Can be given IV

🌤️ Intermediate-Acting:

🔹 NPH, cloudy

🔹 Peaks in 4 to 12 hours

🌙 Long-Acting:

🔹 Glargine, detemir

🔹 No real peak

🔹 Never mix with other insulins

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Food must be ready before rapid-acting insulin

✅ Watch for hypoglycemia at the peak

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

LISPRO = LIGHTNING fast!

👶 Newborn hearts beat FAST, but how fast is normal?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pediatric question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.

.

✅ Correct Answer: D — 110 to 160/min

🧠 Rationale: A normal newborn heart rate is about 110 to 160/min.

It may drop to about 100 while asleep and rise with crying.

Count the apical pulse for a full minute.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Newborn Vital Signs

❤️ Heart Rate:

🔹 110 to 160/min

🔹 Apical pulse for 1 full minute

🫁 Respirations:

🔹 30 to 60/min

🔹 Short pauses under 20 seconds can be normal

🌡️ Temperature:

🔹 Axillary 97.7 to 99.5°F

🔹 Keep baby warm: skin to skin

🚑 When to escalate:

🔹 Heart rate under 100 while awake

🔹 Grunting, flaring or retractions

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Newborns run 110 to 160: think a fast little engine!

Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #327!

🤰 Some pregnancy changes are normal. One of these is NOT!

This is a HIGH-YIELD maternity question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — BP 152/98 mmHg with protein in urine

🧠 Rationale: Preeclampsia is new BP of 140/90 or higher after 20 weeks.

It often comes with protein in the urine.

Mild ankle swelling, a slightly faster heart rate and frequent urination are normal in pregnancy.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Preeclampsia

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 BP 140/90 or higher after 20 weeks

🔹 Protein in urine

🔹 Headache or vision changes

🔹 Upper right belly pain

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Check BP and urine protein

✅ Monitor reflexes

✅ Watch for seizures

💊 Treatment:

🔹 Magnesium sulfate prevents seizures

🔹 Calcium gluconate is the antidote

🚑 When to escalate:

🔹 Severe headache, blurred vision or BP 160/110 or higher

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

After 20 weeks, 140/90 plus protein = think PREECLAMPSIA!

🧠 Rationale: Olanzapine is a second generation (atypical) antipsychotic.

It often causes weight gain, high blood sugar and high cholesterol.

This is called metabolic syndrome.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Olanzapine (Zyprexa)

💊 Drug Class:

🔹 Second generation antipsychotic

❤️ Primary Use:

🔹 Schizophrenia

🔹 Bipolar disorder

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 Weight gain

🔹 High blood sugar

🔹 High cholesterol

🔹 Drowsiness

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Check weight and BMI often

✅ Monitor glucose and lipids

✅ Teach healthy diet and exercise

🚑 When to escalate:

🔹 High fever with rigid muscles: possible NMS

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

ZYPREXA = Zzz and eXtra weight!

#315Pharmacology · post around 08:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #315!

💊 Everyone takes it, but do you know the safe daily limit?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — 4 grams

🧠 Rationale: For most healthy adults, the max is 4 grams (4,000 mg) in 24 hours.

Too much can cause severe liver damage.

Lower limits are used for liver disease or heavy alcohol use.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Acetaminophen

💊 Drug Class:

🔹 Analgesic and antipyretic

❤️ Primary Use:

🔹 Mild pain and fever

⚠️ Overdose Signs:

🔹 Nausea and vomiting early

🔹 Right upper abdominal pain

🔹 Jaundice and rising liver enzymes later

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ Check labels: many combo products contain it

✅ Do not go over the daily max

✅ Limit alcohol

🚑 Antidote:

🔹 Acetylcysteine

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

FOUR is the ceiling: never more than 4 grams in a day!

#316Cardiac · post around 10:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #316!

❤️ Seconds count in a code. Where do you check the pulse?

This is a HIGH-YIELD cardiac emergency question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: D — Carotid pulse

🧠 Rationale: The carotid pulse is checked in adults during CPR.

It is a large central artery that stays palpable when peripheral pulses are lost.

Check for no more than 10 seconds before starting compressions.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Adult CPR Basics

❤️ Pulse Check:

🔹 Adult and child: carotid

🔹 Infant: brachial

🔹 10 seconds max

🚨 Compressions:

✅ 100 to 120 per minute

✅ At least 2 inches deep in adults

✅ Allow full chest recoil

✅ 30 compressions to 2 breaths without an advanced airway

🚑 When to Escalate:

🔹 Call for help and an AED right away

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Carotid for the CENTER of the action: adults get the neck, infants get the arm!

#317Respiratory · post around 12:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #317!

🫁 Look at the chest shape. What does long-term emphysema do?

This is a HIGH-YIELD respiratory question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Barrel-shaped chest

🧠 Rationale: Emphysema traps air in the lungs and causes hyperinflation.

Over time the chest widens front to back, giving a barrel shape.

Pink frothy sputum points to pulmonary edema, not emphysema.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Emphysema

🫁 What Happens:

🔹 Alveoli lose elasticity

🔹 Air gets trapped

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Barrel chest

🔹 Pursed-lip breathing

🔹 Use of accessory muscles

🔹 Thin build, tripod position

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Upright or tripod position

✅ Low-flow oxygen as ordered

✅ Small, high-calorie meals

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Emphysema = trapped air = a chest shaped like a BARREL full of air!

#318Endocrine · post around 15:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #318!

💉 Insulin pens look simple, but one step gets skipped all the time. Do you know it?

This is a HIGH-YIELD endocrine question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Prime the pen with 2 units

🧠 Rationale: Priming with an air shot of 2 units clears air and makes sure the needle works.

Skipping it can lead to a smaller dose than ordered.

Use a new needle every time and hold the pen in place about 10 seconds after injecting.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Insulin Pen Technique

💉 Steps:

✅ Wash hands, check the label and expiration

✅ Roll cloudy insulin gently, never shake

✅ Attach a new needle

✅ Prime 2 units until a drop appears

✅ Dial the dose and inject

✅ Hold 10 seconds, then remove

⚠️ Storage:

🔹 Unopened pens in the fridge

🔹 Never freeze

🚨 Teaching:

✅ Rotate sites

✅ Never share pens

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

PRIME before you DIAL: an air shot every time!

💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #319!

👶 This simple habit saves infant lives. Do you know the rule?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pediatric safety question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — On the back

🧠 Rationale: Healthy infants should be placed on their back for every sleep.

Back sleeping lowers the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).

Pillows, blankets and soft toys should stay out of the crib.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Infant Safe Sleep

👶 Safe Sleep Rules:

✅ Back to sleep, every time

✅ Firm, flat mattress

✅ Nothing soft in the crib

✅ Room share, not bed share

⚠️ Risk Factors:

🔹 Stomach or side sleeping

🔹 Overheating

🔹 Smoke exposure

🚨 Teaching:

✅ Supervised tummy time while awake

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Back to sleep, tummy to play!

🤰 Baby's kicks tell a story. How many should mom feel?

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

✅ Correct Answer: D — 10 movements within 2 hours

🧠 Rationale: A common guideline is at least 10 fetal movements within 2 hours.

Count when the baby is usually active, often after a meal.

Fewer movements than usual should be reported right away.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Fetal Kick Counts

🤰 How to Count:

✅ Lie on the left side

✅ Count kicks, rolls and flutters

✅ Same time each day

⚠️ Report:

🔹 Fewer than 10 in 2 hours

🔹 A clear drop from the usual pattern

🚨 Next Steps:

🔹 Nonstress test may be ordered

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

TEN in TWO: ten kicks in two hours keeps worry away!

Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #321!

🗣️ Therapeutic communication trips up so many students. Which one is right?

This is a HIGH-YIELD mental health question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Tell me more about what you're feeling.

🧠 Rationale: An open-ended statement invites the client to share more.

"Why" questions can sound judgmental and make clients defensive.

False reassurance and "I know how you feel" shut the conversation down.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Therapeutic Communication

✅ Therapeutic:

🔹 Open-ended questions

🔹 Reflecting feelings

🔹 Silence and active listening

🔹 Clarifying

❌ Nontherapeutic:

🔹 "Why" questions

🔹 False reassurance

🔹 Giving advice

🔹 Changing the subject

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Keep it OPEN and about THEM: feelings first, fixes later!

#308Pharmacology · post around 08:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #308!

🍷 Once a week, not once a day. Do you know the big methotrexate rules?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Avoid alcohol while taking this medicine

🧠 Rationale: Methotrexate can damage the liver, and alcohol adds to that risk.

It is taken once a week for RA. Daily dosing by mistake can be fatal.

Folic acid is often given to reduce side effects, and live vaccines are avoided.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Methotrexate

💊 Drug Class:

🔹 Antimetabolite, DMARD (disease-modifying drug for RA)

⚠️ Adverse Effects:

🔹 Liver toxicity

🔹 Bone marrow suppression, infection risk

🔹 Mouth sores and nausea

🔹 Harmful in pregnancy

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ Take on the SAME day once a week

✅ No alcohol

✅ Keep lab appointments: CBC, liver and kidney tests

✅ Report fever, sore throat or mouth sores

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Metho-TREX-ate for RA: once a WEEK, never every day!

#309Cardiac · post around 10:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #309!

🦵 Veins or arteries? This leg finding gives it away!

This is a HIGH-YIELD cardiovascular question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Brown skin discoloration around the ankles

🧠 Rationale: In venous insufficiency, blood pools in the lower legs.

Red blood cells leak into the tissue and leave brown staining near the ankles.

Shiny hairless skin, weak pulses and pain eased by dangling the legs point to arterial disease.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Venous vs Arterial Disease

🩸 Venous Signs:

🔹 Brown discoloration, swelling

🔹 Warm skin, normal pulses

🔹 Ulcers near the inner ankle

❤️ Arterial Signs:

🔹 Shiny, hairless, cool skin

🔹 Weak or absent pulses

🔹 Ulcers on toes, pain with walking

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Venous: ELEVATE legs, use compression

✅ Arterial: keep legs dependent, no compression

✅ Teach to avoid crossing legs

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Venous = Very swollen, Elevate. Arterial = Away from heart, Dangle.

#310Respiratory · post around 12:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #310!

🌬️ Controller or rescue? Students mix this one up all the time!

This is a HIGH-YIELD respiratory question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — "I take it every day, even when I feel fine."

🧠 Rationale: Montelukast is a leukotriene receptor blocker used to prevent asthma symptoms.

It must be taken daily to work, even on good days.

It does not stop a sudden attack. A rescue inhaler like albuterol does that.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Montelukast

💊 Drug Class:

🔹 Leukotriene receptor antagonist (controller)

❤️ Primary Use:

🔹 Long-term asthma control

🔹 Allergic rhinitis

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 Headache

🔹 Mood or behavior changes: report right away

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ Take once daily, usually in the evening

✅ Keep albuterol for sudden symptoms

✅ Do not stop without talking to the provider

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Montelukast = Maintenance. Albuterol = Attack.

#311Endocrine · post around 15:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #311!

❄️ Fridge, freezer or counter? Where does insulin belong?

This is a HIGH-YIELD endocrine question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Keep unopened vials in the refrigerator

🧠 Rationale: Unopened insulin is stored in the refrigerator until the expiration date.

An opened vial can stay at room temperature for about 28 days for most types.

Never freeze insulin, and roll cloudy insulin gently instead of shaking it.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Insulin Storage

🧊 Storage:

🔹 Unopened: refrigerator

🔹 In use: room temperature, most types about 28 days

🔹 Never freeze, keep out of heat and sun

⚠️ Discard If:

🔹 It was frozen or overheated

🔹 Clear insulin looks cloudy

🔹 Past the date or open too long

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ Write the open date on the vial

✅ Roll NPH gently between hands

✅ Room-temperature insulin stings less

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Fridge to store, room temp to use, freezer NEVER!

Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #312!

🥤 One common diet drink ingredient is a big NO in this condition!

This is a HIGH-YIELD pediatric question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Diet soda with aspartame

🧠 Rationale: In PKU, the body cannot break down phenylalanine.

Aspartame turns into phenylalanine, so it must be avoided.

High levels can harm brain development, so a low-phenylalanine diet is lifelong.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Phenylketonuria (PKU)

🧬 What It Is:

🔹 Inherited enzyme defect

🔹 Found on the newborn screen

⚠️ Avoid:

🔹 Aspartame

🔹 High-protein foods: meat, eggs, milk, nuts

✅ Allowed:

✅ Special PKU formula

✅ Most fruits and vegetables in planned amounts

✅ Low-protein breads and pastas

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Teach label reading

✅ Monitor phenylalanine levels

✅ Refer to a dietitian

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

PKU = Please Keep Unsweetened by aspartame!

Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #313!

💉 Rubella vaccine after birth: what is the one big teaching point?

This is a HIGH-YIELD maternity question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Avoid becoming pregnant for 4 weeks

🧠 Rationale: MMR is a live virus vaccine.

It is given after birth when the client is not immune, because it is not given during pregnancy.

Pregnancy should be avoided for 4 weeks. Breastfeeding and newborn contact are safe.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Postpartum Rubella Vaccine

💊 Vaccine Type:

🔹 Live, attenuated MMR (measles, mumps, rubella)

🤰 Why It Matters:

🔹 Rubella in pregnancy can cause birth defects

🔹 Not given during pregnancy

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ Avoid pregnancy for 4 weeks

✅ Breastfeeding is safe

✅ Mild rash or joint aches can happen

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Live vaccine = Leave pregnancy plans for 4 weeks.

Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #314!

😰 Racing heart, fast breathing, sudden fear. What is your FIRST move?

This is a HIGH-YIELD mental health question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: D — Stay with the client and speak calmly

🧠 Rationale: During a panic attack, the client cannot focus or learn new information.

Staying with the client and using short, calm statements gives safety.

Teaching and exploring the cause come later, once anxiety goes down.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Panic Attacks

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Racing heart, chest tightness

🔹 Rapid breathing, dizziness

🔹 Intense fear or feeling of doom

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Stay with the client

✅ Use short, simple, calm words

✅ Move to a quiet, low-stimulus area

✅ Coach slow breathing

📝 Later:

✅ Teach coping skills when calm

✅ Explore triggers together

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Panic = Presence first, Problem-solving later.

#301Pharmacology · post around 08:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #301!

🧪 Peak or trough? Timing the vancomycin lab matters!

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Within 30 minutes before the next dose

🧠 Rationale: The trough is the lowest drug level in the blood.

It is drawn just before the next dose, usually within 30 minutes.

Drawing it at the wrong time gives a false result and a wrong dose change.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Vancomycin

💊 Drug Class:

🔹 Glycopeptide antibiotic (used for MRSA and C. diff)

⚠️ Adverse Effects:

🔹 Kidney injury (nephrotoxicity)

🔹 Hearing loss or ringing in the ears

🔹 Flushing and rash if infused too fast

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Infuse slowly, over at least 60 minutes

✅ Monitor creatinine and urine output

✅ Time trough draws right before the dose

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Trough = Toward the next dose. Lowest level, last minute!
