#302Cardiac · post around 10:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #302!

❤️ Can you find the mitral valve on the chest?

This is a HIGH-YIELD cardiac assessment question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: D — 5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line

🧠 Rationale: The mitral valve is best heard at the apex of the heart.

This is the 5th intercostal space at the left midclavicular line.

It is also where the apical pulse is counted.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Heart Sound Landmarks

🩺 Valve Areas:

🔹 Aortic: 2nd ICS, right sternal border

🔹 Pulmonic: 2nd ICS, left sternal border

🔹 Tricuspid: 4th ICS, left lower sternal border

🔹 Mitral: 5th ICS, left midclavicular line

🔊 Heart Sounds:

🔹 S1 (lub) is loudest at the apex

🔹 S2 (dub) is loudest at the base

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Count the apical pulse for a full minute

✅ Listen with the diaphragm, then the bell

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

All People Enjoy Time Magazine: Aortic, Pulmonic, Erb's point, Tricuspid, Mitral!

#303Respiratory · post around 12:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #303!

🫁 When does your client actually need suctioning?

This is a HIGH-YIELD respiratory question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Coarse crackles over the large airways

🧠 Rationale: Coarse crackles (rhonchi) mean secretions are in the large airways.

Suction is done based on assessment, not on a set schedule.

The other findings are normal and do not need suctioning.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Airway Suctioning

⚠️ Signs a Client Needs Suctioning:

🔹 Coarse crackles or gurgling

🔹 Visible secretions

🔹 Falling SpO2

🔹 Restlessness or increased work of breathing

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Preoxygenate before suctioning

✅ Suction no longer than 10 to 15 seconds

✅ Apply suction only while pulling out

✅ Reassess breath sounds after

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Hear the gurgle, clear the gurgle!

#304Endocrine · post around 15:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #304!

🦴 Calcium and phosphorus: which way do they go?

This is a HIGH-YIELD endocrine question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — High calcium, low phosphorus

🧠 Rationale: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) pulls calcium out of the bones.

PTH also makes the kidneys get rid of phosphorus.

Calcium and phosphorus move in opposite directions.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Hyperparathyroidism

⚠️ Signs and Symptoms:

🔹 Kidney stones

🔹 Bone pain and fractures

🔹 Muscle weakness and fatigue

🔹 Constipation and confusion

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Encourage fluids to prevent stones

✅ Strain urine if stones suspected

✅ Fall and fracture precautions

✅ Monitor calcium levels

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Stones, bones, groans and moans: high calcium!

#305Peds · post around 17:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #305!

🚗 Rear-facing car seats: when is it safe to turn around?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pediatric safety question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — As long as possible, until the seat's limits

🧠 Rationale: Rear-facing seats protect the head, neck and spine in a crash.

Children should stay rear-facing until they reach the seat's height or weight limit.

Most children can stay rear-facing well past age 2.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Car Seat Safety

🚸 Key Points:

🔹 Rear-facing as long as the seat allows

🔹 Then forward-facing with a harness

🔹 Then a booster seat until the seat belt fits

🔹 Back seat until at least age 13

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ Harness snug at the collarbone

✅ Chest clip at armpit level

✅ No bulky coats under the harness

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Rear-facing is the safest-facing!

#306Maternity · post around 19:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #306!

🤰 Preterm labor at 30 weeks: which drug protects the baby's lungs?

This is a HIGH-YIELD maternity question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Betamethasone

🧠 Rationale: Betamethasone is a corticosteroid given to the mother.

It speeds up fetal lung maturity and surfactant production.

It lowers the risk of newborn respiratory distress syndrome.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Betamethasone in Preterm Labor

💊 Drug Class:

🔹 Corticosteroid

❤️ Primary Use:

🔹 Fetal lung maturity, usually 24 to 34 weeks

🔹 Given IM, 2 doses 24 hours apart

⚠️ Watch For:

🔹 Raised blood glucose in the mother

🧠 Do Not Confuse:

🔹 Magnesium sulfate protects the fetal brain

🔹 Oxytocin and methylergonovine are for contractions and bleeding

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Beta for Breathing: betamethasone builds baby's lungs!

#307Mental Health · post around 21:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #307!

🧠 Delirium or dementia? This one shows up on the NCLEX a lot!

This is a HIGH-YIELD mental health question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Sudden onset over hours to days

🧠 Rationale: Delirium comes on suddenly, over hours to days.

It is often caused by infection, drugs, dehydration or low oxygen.

It is usually reversible once the cause is treated.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Delirium vs Dementia

⚡ Delirium:

🔹 Sudden onset

🔹 Attention changes and fluctuates

🔹 Often reversible

🐢 Dementia:

🔹 Slow, gradual decline

🔹 Attention intact early

🔹 Progressive, not reversible

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Report new confusion right away

✅ Look for the cause: UTI, meds, hypoxia

✅ Reorient, keep a calm, safe room

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Delirium is Dramatic and Sudden. Dementia is Drawn out!

#294Pharmacology · post around 08:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #294!

🥬 Warfarin and leafy greens. Do you have to give up salad?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Keep vitamin K intake consistent

🧠 Rationale: Vitamin K reverses the effect of warfarin.

Clients do not need to avoid greens. Big changes in intake make the INR swing.

Steady, consistent intake keeps the dose working the same way each day.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Warfarin (Coumadin)

💊 Drug Class:

🔹 Oral anticoagulant (vitamin K antagonist)

📊 Lab to Monitor:

🔹 PT/INR, usual goal 2 to 3 for most clients

⚠️ Signs of Bleeding:

🔹 Bleeding gums or nosebleeds

🔹 Black, tarry stools

🔹 Blood in urine

🔹 Easy bruising

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ Keep vitamin K foods steady

✅ Use a soft toothbrush and electric razor

✅ Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs unless approved

✅ Wear a medical alert ID

🚑 Antidote:

🔹 Vitamin K (phytonadione)

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Warfarin likes routine: same greens, same INR!

#295Cardiac · post around 10:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #295!

❤️ One ECG change that means time is muscle. Can you spot it?

This is a HIGH-YIELD cardiac question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — ST-segment elevation

🧠 Rationale: ST elevation shows acute injury to the heart muscle.

Peaked T waves point to high potassium. Sawtooth waves mean atrial flutter.

Prominent U waves point to low potassium.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Myocardial Infarction

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Crushing chest pain or pressure

🔹 Pain to jaw, neck or left arm

🔹 Shortness of breath and sweating

🔹 Women may have fatigue or nausea

📊 Diagnostics:

🔹 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes

🔹 Troponin is the most specific lab

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Get a 12-lead ECG right away

✅ Give aspirin as ordered

✅ Oxygen if SpO2 is below 90%

✅ Nitroglycerin and pain control as ordered

🚑 Emergency:

🔹 STEMI needs fast reperfusion, often a cath lab

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

ST up? Get the cath lab up!

#296Infection Control · post around 12:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #296!

🫁 TB skin test day. Do you measure the redness or the bump?

This is a HIGH-YIELD infection control question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Induration of 10 mm

🧠 Rationale: Read the test in 48 to 72 hours.

Measure only the raised, hard area (induration), not the redness.

For health care workers, 10 mm or more is positive.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: TB Skin Test (Mantoux)

📏 Positive Results:

🔹 5 mm or more: HIV, immunosuppressed, close contacts

🔹 10 mm or more: health care workers, recent immigrants

🔹 15 mm or more: no known risk factors

💉 How It Is Given:

🔹 Intradermal injection on the inner forearm

🔹 Forms a small bleb

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Do not rub or cover the site

✅ Measure induration in mm

✅ Positive test needs a chest X-ray

⚠️ Remember:

🔹 Positive test shows exposure, not always active disease

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Feel the bump, ignore the blush!

#297Endocrine · post around 15:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #297!

🩸 High sugar or low sugar? Can you tell them apart?

This is a HIGH-YIELD endocrine question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Increased thirst and urination

🧠 Rationale: High glucose spills into the urine and pulls water with it.

This causes polyuria, then thirst (polydipsia).

Shakiness, sweating, clammy skin and hunger point to hypoglycemia.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Hyperglycemia vs Hypoglycemia

📈 Hyperglycemia Signs:

🔹 Polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia

🔹 Hot, dry skin

🔹 Blurred vision and fatigue

📉 Hypoglycemia Signs:

🔹 Shaky, sweaty, cool and clammy

🔹 Hunger and anxiety

🔹 Confusion if severe

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Check glucose first

✅ Low and awake: 15 g fast carbs, recheck in 15 min

✅ High: follow insulin orders, check ketones

🚑 When to Escalate:

🔹 Unconscious client: glucagon or IV dextrose

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Hot and dry, sugar high. Cold and clammy, need some candy!

👶 Fresh cleft lip repair. How should this baby lie?

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Position the infant on the back or side

🧠 Rationale: Lying prone lets the face rub the bed and damage the repair.

Back or side lying protects the suture line.

Avoid pacifiers and anything that puts tension on the lip.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Cleft Lip Repair

🍼 Feeding:

🔹 Special nipples or syringe feeding as ordered

🔹 Burp often, they swallow air

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Elbow restraints to keep hands away

✅ No pacifiers or straws

✅ Clean the suture line as ordered

✅ Manage pain and crying

⚠️ Watch For:

🔹 Redness or drainage at the site

🔹 Signs of aspiration with feeds

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Lip repair? Baby faces the sky, not the bed!

🧠 Rationale: CN XI moves the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid.

Test it with shoulder shrugs and turning the head against resistance.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Cranial Nerve Testing

🔹 Quick Tests:

🔹 CN V: clench jaw, light touch on face

🔹 CN VII: smile, raise eyebrows

🔹 CN XI: shrug shoulders, turn head

🔹 CN XII: stick out tongue

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Compare left and right sides

✅ Report new weakness right away

⚠️ Red Flag:

🔹 Sudden one-sided weakness can mean stroke

Eleven helps you shrug and say 'I don't know!'

#300Safety · post around 21:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #300!

🍽️ Stroke client at mealtime. One move keeps food out of the lungs.

This is a HIGH-YIELD safety question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Tuck the chin when swallowing

🧠 Rationale: Tucking the chin helps protect the airway.

Tilting the head back opens the airway and raises aspiration risk.

Straws and thin liquids move too fast for a weak swallow.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Aspiration Prevention

⚠️ Signs of Aspiration:

🔹 Coughing or choking with meals

🔹 Wet, gurgly voice

🔹 Fever or crackles later

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Swallow screen before any food

✅ Sit upright at 90 degrees

✅ Thickened liquids as ordered

✅ Small bites, unaffected side

✅ Stay upright 30 minutes after meals

🩺 Team:

🔹 Speech therapy evaluates swallowing

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Chin down, food down!

#287Pharmacology · post around 08:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #287!

💉 Two insulins, one syringe. Which one goes in first?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Draw up regular insulin first

🧠 Rationale: Regular insulin is clear. NPH is cloudy.

Draw up clear before cloudy so NPH never gets into the regular vial.

Roll the NPH vial gently. Never shake it.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Mixing Insulin

💊 Insulin Types:

🔹 Regular: short acting, clear

🔹 NPH: intermediate acting, cloudy

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Inject air into NPH first, then regular

✅ Draw up regular, then NPH

✅ Roll NPH gently, do not shake

✅ Never mix glargine with other insulins

⚠️ Watch For:

🔹 Hypoglycemia at each insulin's peak

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Clear before cloudy!

💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #288!

❤️ Sawtooth waves on the monitor. Can you name the rhythm?

This is a HIGH-YIELD cardiac question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Atrial flutter

🧠 Rationale: Atrial flutter shows regular sawtooth flutter waves.

Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with no clear P waves.

V tach shows wide, fast QRS complexes.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Atrial Flutter

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Palpitations

🔹 Shortness of breath

🔹 Fatigue or dizziness

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Check the client and vital signs first

✅ Expect rate control meds

✅ Anticoagulation to lower stroke risk

🚑 Escalate:

🔹 Unstable client may need cardioversion

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Flutter = sawtooth. Fib = fuzzy and irregular.

#289Renal · post around 12:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #289!

🫘 One lab tells you the most about the kidneys. Which one?

This is a HIGH-YIELD renal question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Serum creatinine

🧠 Rationale: Creatinine comes from muscle at a steady rate.

Only the kidneys clear it, so it tracks kidney function best.

BUN can rise from dehydration, high protein or GI bleeding.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Kidney Labs

🧪 Normal Ranges (adult):

🔹 Creatinine: about 0.6 to 1.3 mg/dL

🔹 BUN: about 10 to 20 mg/dL

⚠️ Rising Creatinine Can Mean:

🔹 Acute kidney injury

🔹 Chronic kidney disease

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Track intake and output

✅ Check doses of kidney-cleared drugs

✅ Report a rising trend

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Creatinine = the kidney's report card!

👶 First steps! When do most kids start walking on their own?

Cruising along furniture often starts around 9 to 10 months.

Not walking by 18 months needs follow-up.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Gross Motor Milestones

📅 Key Milestones:

🔹 Rolls over: 4 to 6 months

🔹 Sits without support: about 6 months

🔹 Pulls to stand: 9 to 10 months

🔹 Walks alone: 12 to 15 months

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Ask parents about milestones at each visit

✅ Report delays for screening

✅ Teach home safety as mobility grows

Turn one, take a step, have some fun!

💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #291!

🧠 This Parkinson med and your dinner plate do not mix well. Why?

This is a HIGH-YIELD neuro pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Avoid large high-protein meals near doses

🧠 Rationale: Protein competes with levodopa for absorption into the body and brain.

Large high-protein meals near doses can weaken the effect.

Never stop the drug suddenly.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Carbidopa-Levodopa

💊 Drug Class: Dopamine precursor combination

❤️ Primary Use: Parkinson disease

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 Orthostatic hypotension

🔹 Nausea

🔹 Involuntary movements

🔹 Dark urine or sweat, harmless

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ Rise slowly

✅ Do not stop suddenly

✅ Report new jerky movements

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Levodopa and steak? Keep them apart!

✅ BP 140/90 or higher

💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #293!

🧩 Who is really angry here? Name that defense mechanism!

This is a HIGH-YIELD mental health question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Projection

🧠 Rationale: Projection means putting your own feelings onto someone else.

The client is angry but says the coworker hates them.

The feeling belongs to the client, not the coworker.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Defense Mechanisms

🧠 Know These:

🔹 Denial: refusing to accept reality

🔹 Projection: blaming your feelings on others

🔹 Regression: acting younger under stress

🔹 Sublimation: turning urges into healthy activity

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Stay calm and nonjudgmental

✅ Help the client name their own feelings

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Projection = a movie projector. Your feelings show up on someone else's screen!

#280Pharmacology · post around 08:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #280!

🍷 One drink with this antibiotic can make a client very sick. Do you know which rule?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Avoid alcohol during and after therapy

🧠 Rationale: Metronidazole plus alcohol can cause a disulfiram-like reaction.

Signs include flushing, nausea, vomiting and a fast heart rate.

Avoid alcohol during therapy and for at least 3 days after the last dose.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Metronidazole

💊 Drug Class: Nitroimidazole antibiotic and antiprotozoal

❤️ Primary Use: C. diff, anaerobic infections, trichomoniasis, giardia

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 Metallic taste

🔹 Nausea

🔹 Dark urine

🔹 Numbness or tingling with long use

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ No alcohol, including mouthwash with alcohol

✅ Finish the full course

✅ Report numbness or seizures

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Metro + booze = big trouble!

#281Cardiac · post around 10:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #281!

🦵 One leg is swollen and warm after surgery. What are you looking at?

This is a HIGH-YIELD cardiovascular question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Swelling and warmth of the left calf

🧠 Rationale: A DVT blocks venous return in one leg.

Expect swelling, warmth, redness and calf pain on that side.

A cool, pale, pulseless leg points to an arterial problem instead.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Deep Vein Thrombosis

❤️ Risk Factors: Surgery, bed rest, long travel, pregnancy, estrogen, smoking

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Swelling of one leg

🔹 Warmth and redness

🔹 Calf pain or tenderness

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Do not massage the leg

✅ Give anticoagulants as prescribed

✅ Early ambulation to prevent DVT

✅ SCDs only on the unaffected leg

🚑 Emergency: Sudden chest pain and shortness of breath may mean a PE. Call the rapid response team.

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Never rub a clot!

#282Respiratory · post around 12:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #282!

🔥 The pulse ox reads 99%, but this client is in danger. Do you know why?

This is a HIGH-YIELD respiratory question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Give 100% oxygen by nonrebreather mask

🧠 Rationale: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin much more tightly than oxygen.

Pulse oximetry cannot tell the difference, so SpO2 looks falsely normal.

100% oxygen speeds removal of carbon monoxide from the blood.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Carbon Monoxide Poisoning

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Headache

🔹 Dizziness and confusion

🔹 Nausea

🔹 Cherry red skin (late sign)

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Give 100% O2 by nonrebreather

✅ Check carboxyhemoglobin level

✅ Monitor neuro status

✅ Hyperbaric oxygen if severe

🏠 Patient Teaching:

✅ Install CO detectors at home

✅ Have heaters checked yearly

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

CO fools the pulse ox. Trust the symptoms!

🤰 Halfway there! Where should the fundus be at 20 weeks?

This is a HIGH-YIELD maternity question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

✅ Correct Answer: B — At the umbilicus

🧠 Rationale: At 20 weeks the fundus is usually at the level of the umbilicus.

From 20 to about 36 weeks, fundal height in cm roughly matches the weeks of pregnancy.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Fundal Height

📏 Landmarks:

🔹 12 weeks: just above the symphysis pubis

🔹 20 weeks: at the umbilicus

🔹 36 weeks: near the xiphoid process

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Client voids before measuring

✅ Measure from symphysis to top of fundus

✅ Report a size 3 cm or more off dates

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

20 weeks, 20 cm, belly button!

🏃 This client is too busy to sit down and eat. What do you do?

This is a HIGH-YIELD mental health question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

✅ Correct Answer: A — Offer high-calorie finger foods

🧠 Rationale: Clients in mania burn a lot of energy and have trouble sitting still.

High-calorie, high-protein finger foods can be eaten on the go.

Forcing the client to sit can increase agitation.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Mania

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Little need for sleep

🔹 Racing thoughts and fast speech

🔹 Grandiosity

🔹 Constant movement

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Low-stimulation environment

✅ Finger foods and fluids often

✅ Short, clear statements

✅ Monitor weight and sleep

💊 Common Meds: Lithium, valproate, atypical antipsychotics

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Mania on the move? Food that moves too!

Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #285!

🕯️ Home oxygen saves lives, but one mistake can start a fire. Which rule is right?

This is a HIGH-YIELD safety question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: D — Keep the oxygen away from open flames

🧠 Rationale: Oxygen is not flammable, but it makes fire burn hotter and faster.

No smoking, candles, gas stoves or open flames near oxygen.

Use water-based products, not petroleum jelly.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Home Oxygen Safety

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ Post No Smoking signs

✅ Keep away from heat sources

✅ Use water-based lip and nose products

✅ Do not change the flow rate without an order

⚠️ Hazards:

🔹 Cigarettes and candles

🔹 Gas stoves and fireplaces

🔹 Petroleum or oil-based products

🚑 Emergency: Shut off oxygen and leave the room if a fire starts.

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

O2 and fire never share a room!

#286Peds · post around 21:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #286!

👶 48 hours and still no first stool. What could this be?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pediatric question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Hirschsprung disease

🧠 Rationale: Hirschsprung disease means part of the colon has no nerve cells.

Stool cannot move through, so meconium is delayed and the belly distends.

Most newborns pass meconium within 24 to 48 hours.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Hirschsprung Disease

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 No meconium in 24 to 48 hours

🔹 Abdominal distention

🔹 Bilious vomiting

🔹 Ribbon-like, foul stools in older kids

🔬 Diagnosis: Rectal biopsy showing no ganglion cells

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Measure abdominal girth

✅ Report fever or explosive diarrhea

✅ Prepare family for surgery

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

No nerves, no movement!

#273Pharmacology · post around 08:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #273!

💉 One tiny bubble in this syringe is supposed to be there. Do you know why?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Do not expel the air bubble

🧠 Rationale: Enoxaparin is a low molecular weight heparin.

The air bubble in the prefilled syringe helps make sure the full dose is given.

Do not aspirate or rub the site, since both increase bruising.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Enoxaparin

💊 Drug Class: Low molecular weight heparin

❤️ Primary Use: Prevent and treat DVT and PE

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 Bleeding and bruising

🔹 Low platelets

🔹 Injection site pain

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ Inject in the abdomen, 2 inches from the navel

✅ Rotate sites

✅ Do not rub the site

✅ Report black stools or unusual bleeding

🚑 Antidote: Protamine sulfate (partial reversal)

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Keep the bubble, skip the rub!

#274Cardiac · post around 10:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #274!

❤️ Left side or right side? This one trips up so many students!

This is a HIGH-YIELD cardiac question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Crackles in the lungs

🧠 Rationale: When the left ventricle fails, blood backs up into the lungs.

This causes crackles, dyspnea and orthopnea.

JVD, ascites and an enlarged liver point to right-sided failure.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Left-Sided Heart Failure

🫁 Where Fluid Goes: Back into the lungs

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Crackles

🔹 Dyspnea and orthopnea

🔹 Pink frothy sputum (severe)

🔹 Fatigue

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ High Fowler position

✅ Give oxygen as ordered

✅ Give diuretics as ordered

✅ Daily weights and strict I and O

🚑 Escalate: Pink frothy sputum or sudden worsening dyspnea

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Left = Lungs. Right = Rest of the body.

#275Endocrine · post around 12:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #275!

🦋 Everything slows down with this thyroid problem. Can you spot it?

This is a HIGH-YIELD endocrine question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Cold intolerance and weight gain

🧠 Rationale: Hypothyroidism slows the body's metabolism.

Clients feel cold, gain weight and feel tired.

Heat intolerance, weight loss and tremors point to hyperthyroidism.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Hypothyroidism

🧬 Problem: Too little thyroid hormone

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Cold intolerance

🔹 Weight gain

🔹 Fatigue and constipation

🔹 Slow heart rate

🔹 Dry skin and hair loss

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Give levothyroxine every morning on an empty stomach

✅ Keep the client warm

✅ Watch for chest pain when starting thyroid hormone

🚑 Emergency: Myxedema coma, with low temp, low BP and confusion

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Hypo = everything goes LOW and SLOW.

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

✅ Correct Answer: D — Push-pull toy

🧠 Rationale: Toddlers learn through movement and are in the autonomy stage.

Push-pull toys build gross motor skills.

Small pieces are a choking risk, and rule-based games fit school-age children.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Toddler Growth and Development

👶 Age: 1 to 3 years

🧠 Erikson Stage: Autonomy vs shame and doubt

🎈 Type of Play: Parallel play

✅ Good Toys:

🔹 Push-pull toys

🔹 Large blocks

🔹 Stacking toys

🔹 Large crayons

⚠️ Safety:

✅ No small parts, coins or balloons

✅ Avoid grapes and hot dogs unless cut small

🚑 Choking risk is highest in this age group

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Toddlers on the go need toys that go!

#277Maternity · post around 17:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #277!

🤰 This vitamin protects the baby before many people even know they are pregnant!

This is a HIGH-YIELD maternity question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — To prevent neural tube defects

🧠 Rationale: Folic acid lowers the risk of neural tube defects like spina bifida.

The neural tube forms very early, often before a client knows she is pregnant.

That is why folic acid is started before conception.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Folic Acid in Pregnancy

💊 Supplement: Folic acid (vitamin B9)

❤️ Purpose: Prevent neural tube defects

📏 Usual Dose: 400 mcg daily for most clients

🥬 Food Sources:

🔹 Leafy green vegetables

🔹 Fortified cereals

🔹 Beans and lentils

🔹 Citrus fruits

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ Start at least 1 month before pregnancy

✅ Continue through early pregnancy

🚑 Higher Dose: Clients with a prior neural tube defect pregnancy, as ordered

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Folic acid = Fold the neural tube right!

🧠 Therapeutic communication questions are all over the NCLEX. Pick the best response!

This is a HIGH-YIELD mental health question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — You seem anxious. Tell me what you are feeling.

🧠 Rationale: Naming what the nurse sees and inviting the client to share is therapeutic.

False reassurance and changing the subject block communication.

Why questions can make clients feel defensive.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Therapeutic Communication

✅ Therapeutic Techniques:

🔹 Making observations

🔹 Open-ended questions

🔹 Reflecting feelings

🔹 Silence

⚠️ Nontherapeutic Responses:

🔹 False reassurance

🔹 Asking why

🔹 Changing the subject

🔹 Giving advice

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Stay with the anxious client

✅ Use short, calm sentences

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Focus on FEELINGS, not fixing.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Pain or swelling in the heel

🧠 Rationale: Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic.

These drugs carry a boxed warning for tendinitis and tendon rupture, most often the Achilles tendon.

Heel pain or swelling means stop exercise and call the provider right away.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Ciprofloxacin

💊 Drug Class: Fluoroquinolone antibiotic

❤️ Primary Use: UTIs and other bacterial infections

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 Tendon pain or rupture

🔹 Nausea and diarrhea

🔹 Sun sensitivity

🔹 Dizziness

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ Report heel or tendon pain right away

✅ Drink plenty of fluids

✅ Take 2 hours before or 6 hours after antacids, iron or calcium

✅ Use sunscreen

🚑 Higher Risk: Older adults, steroid use, kidney, heart or lung transplant

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Cipro? Protect the heel you go!

💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #267!

🧂 Salt hides in more foods than most clients think. Which answer shows real understanding?

This is a HIGH-YIELD cardiac question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — "I will avoid canned and processed foods."

🧠 Rationale: Sodium makes the body hold on to fluid.

In heart failure, extra fluid strains the heart and causes swelling and shortness of breath.

Canned soups, deli meats, soy sauce and processed foods are some of the biggest sodium sources.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Heart Failure Diet

❤️ Why It Matters: Less sodium means less fluid overload

⚠️ High-Sodium Foods:

🔹 Canned soups and vegetables

🔹 Deli and cured meats

🔹 Soy sauce and pickles

🔹 Frozen and fast foods

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ Read food labels for sodium

✅ Choose fresh foods and season with herbs

✅ Weigh daily at the same time

🚑 Call the Provider: Gain of 2 to 3 lb in a day or 5 lb in a week

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Fresh is best, cans are a salt test!

💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #268!

🩸 One lab value tells you about the last 3 months of blood sugar. Do you know the cutoff?

This is a HIGH-YIELD endocrine question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: D — 6.8%

🧠 Rationale: An A1C of 6.5% or higher meets the criterion for diabetes.

5.7% to 6.4% is prediabetes, and below 5.7% is normal.

Only 6.8% is at or above 6.5%.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Hemoglobin A1C

🩸 What It Shows: Average blood glucose over about 3 months

📊 Ranges:

🔹 Normal: below 5.7%

🔹 Prediabetes: 5.7% to 6.4%

🔹 Diabetes: 6.5% or higher

🎯 Common Goal: Below 7% for many adults with diabetes

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ No fasting needed for this test

✅ Usually checked every 3 to 6 months

✅ Teach that it reflects long-term control

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

6.5 and up, diabetes shows up!

Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #269!

🧠 One bruise in a very specific spot is a big NCLEX clue. Can you spot it?

This is a HIGH-YIELD neuro question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Bruising behind the ears

🧠 Rationale: Bruising behind the ears over the mastoid bone is called Battle sign.

It is a classic sign of a basilar skull fracture.

Bruising around both eyes (raccoon eyes) and clear fluid from the nose or ears are other signs.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Basilar Skull Fracture

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Battle sign: bruising behind the ears

🔹 Raccoon eyes

🔹 Clear fluid from the nose or ears

🔹 Halo sign on gauze

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Do not insert an NG tube through the nose

✅ Do not suction through the nose

✅ Tell the client not to blow the nose

✅ Check fluid for glucose (CSF)

🚑 Watch For: Meningitis and rising ICP

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Battle behind the ears, raccoon around the eyes!

#270Respiratory · post around 17:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #270!

🫁 Bubbles in a chest tube can be normal or a problem. Do you know which chamber matters?

This is a HIGH-YIELD respiratory question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — An air leak in the system

🧠 Rationale: Continuous bubbling in the water seal chamber means an air leak.

Gentle bubbling in the suction control chamber is expected with wet suction.

Intermittent bubbling in the water seal with coughing or exhaling can be normal with a pneumothorax.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Chest Tubes

🫁 Water Seal Chamber:

🔹 Tidaling up and down with breathing is normal

🔹 Continuous bubbling means an air leak

🔹 Tidaling stops when the lung re-expands or the tube kinks

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Check connections from the client to the drain

✅ Keep the drain below the chest

✅ Keep the tubing free of kinks and loops

✅ Never clamp without an order

🚑 Report: Sudden drainage over 100 mL/hr or new trouble breathing

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Water seal bubbling nonstop? Look for the leak!

#271Maternity · post around 19:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #271!

🤰 Lying flat can cause trouble late in pregnancy. What is the quick fix?

This is a HIGH-YIELD maternity question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: D — Turn the client onto her left side

🧠 Rationale: Lying flat lets the heavy uterus press on the inferior vena cava.

Less blood returns to the heart, so blood pressure drops and the client feels dizzy.

Turning to the left side takes pressure off the vena cava and restores blood flow.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Supine Hypotensive Syndrome

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Dizziness and lightheadedness

🔹 Pale, clammy skin

🔹 Low blood pressure

🔹 Fast heart rate

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Turn to the left side

✅ Use a wedge under the right hip if the client must be on her back

✅ Recheck vital signs

✅ Monitor the fetal heart rate

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Feeling faint? Go left, it's great!

💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #272!

🔥 Heartburn every night? One simple habit makes a big difference. Do you know it?

This is a HIGH-YIELD GI question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Avoid lying down for 3 hours after eating

🧠 Rationale: Staying upright for 2 to 3 hours after eating keeps acid in the stomach.

Large meals and lying down after eating increase reflux.

Peppermint, chocolate, caffeine and fatty foods relax the lower esophageal sphincter.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: GERD

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Heartburn after meals

🔹 Sour taste or regurgitation

🔹 Chronic cough or hoarse voice

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ Eat small, frequent meals

✅ Raise the head of the bed 6 to 8 inches

✅ Avoid caffeine, chocolate, peppermint and fatty foods

✅ Stop smoking and limit alcohol

💊 Common Meds: Antacids, H2 blockers, proton pump inhibitors

🚑 Report: Trouble swallowing, vomiting blood or black stools

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Stay up after you sup!

#259Pharmacology · post around 08:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #259!

🦴 One bone medication has some very strict rules. Do you know them?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Take It with a Full Glass of Plain Water

🧠 Rationale: Alendronate must be taken first thing in the morning on an empty stomach.

A full glass of plain water helps it reach the stomach and lowers the risk of esophagus irritation.

Food, coffee and milk block absorption, and lying down can cause esophagitis.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Alendronate

💊 Drug Class: Bisphosphonate

❤️ Primary Use: Preventing and treating osteoporosis

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 Heartburn and esophagus irritation

🔹 Trouble swallowing

🔹 Rare jaw bone problems

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ Take in the morning before food or other meds

✅ Use 6 to 8 oz of plain water only

✅ Stay upright for at least 30 minutes

✅ Wait 30 minutes before eating

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Water, wake, wait upright 30!

#260Cardiac · post around 10:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #260!

❤️ Chest pain in the ED. Which lab tells you it is a heart attack?

This is a HIGH-YIELD cardiac question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Troponin

🧠 Rationale: Troponin is the most specific lab for damage to heart muscle.

It starts to rise within a few hours of a myocardial infarction and stays high for days.

Potassium, hemoglobin and sodium matter, but they do not confirm an MI.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Troponin and MI

❤️ What It Shows: Injury to the heart muscle

⏱️ Timing: Rises within about 3 to 4 hours and stays high up to 2 weeks

⚠️ MI Signs:

🔹 Chest pain or pressure

🔹 Pain to the jaw, arm or back

🔹 Shortness of breath and sweating

🔹 Women may have fatigue or nausea only

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Get a 12 lead ECG within 10 minutes

✅ Draw serial troponins

✅ Give oxygen if SpO2 is low

✅ Give aspirin and nitroglycerin as ordered

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Troponin tells the truth about the heart!

#261Respiratory · post around 12:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #261!

🫁 Suctioning a trach the wrong way can drop oxygen fast. What comes first?

This is a HIGH-YIELD respiratory question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Give 100% Oxygen Before Suctioning

🧠 Rationale: Suctioning removes oxygen along with secretions.

Giving 100% oxygen first helps prevent hypoxia.

Suction is applied only while pulling the catheter out, for 10 to 15 seconds at most.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Tracheostomy Suctioning

🫁 When to Suction: Only when needed, such as noisy breathing, visible secretions or low SpO2

⚠️ Watch For:

🔹 Low oxygen saturation

🔹 Bradycardia or other dysrhythmias

🔹 Airway irritation

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Use sterile technique in the hospital

✅ Hyperoxygenate before and after

✅ Suction 10 to 15 seconds per pass

✅ Rest the client between passes

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Oxygen in, suction out, 15 seconds tops!

💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #262!

🧠 One number tells you a brain injury is severe. Do you know it?

This is a HIGH-YIELD neuro question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: D — 7

🧠 Rationale: A GCS of 8 or less means a severe brain injury.

At this level the client may not be able to protect the airway.

A score of 15 is normal, 13 to 15 is mild and 9 to 12 is moderate.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Glasgow Coma Scale

🧠 What It Measures: Eye opening, verbal response and motor response

📊 Score Range: 3 (lowest) to 15 (normal)

⚠️ Severity:

🔹 13 to 15: mild

🔹 9 to 12: moderate

🔹 8 or less: severe

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Check GCS often and trend the scores

✅ Report any drop of 2 or more points

✅ Protect the airway in low scores

🚑 Emergency: A falling GCS can mean rising ICP. Notify the provider right away.

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Less than 8, intubate!

✅ Correct Answer: A — MMR

🧠 Rationale: MMR is a live vaccine.

Live vaccines can cause infection in a child with a weak immune system.

Inactivated vaccines like the flu shot are not live and may be given per the provider.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Live Vaccines

💉 Common Live Vaccines:

🔹 MMR

🔹 Varicella

🔹 Nasal spray flu vaccine

🔹 Rotavirus

⚠️ Avoid Live Vaccines In:

🔹 Chemotherapy

🔹 High dose steroids

🔹 Pregnancy

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Check immune status before any vaccine

✅ Teach family to keep up with their own vaccines

✅ Review the timing with the oncology team

Weak immune system? No live vaccines!

💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #264!

🍌 A healthy snack can be risky for weak kidneys. Can you spot it?

This is a HIGH-YIELD renal question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: D — Bananas

🧠 Rationale: Bananas are high in potassium.

Damaged kidneys cannot remove extra potassium well.

High potassium can cause dangerous heart rhythms.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Chronic Kidney Disease Diet

🫘 What Happens: The kidneys cannot filter waste, fluid and electrolytes well

⚠️ Foods to Limit:

🔹 High potassium: bananas, oranges, potatoes, tomatoes

🔹 High phosphorus: dairy, colas, processed foods

🔹 High sodium: canned and salty foods

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ Follow fluid limits if ordered

✅ Avoid salt substitutes, which often contain potassium

✅ Take phosphate binders with meals

🚑 Emergency: Muscle weakness or an irregular heartbeat can mean high potassium.

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Bad kidneys, no bananas!

✅ Correct Answer: C — 145/min

🧠 Rationale: The normal fetal heart rate baseline is 110 to 160 beats per minute.

A baseline below 110 is bradycardia.

A baseline above 160 is tachycardia.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Fetal Heart Rate

❤️ Normal Baseline: 110 to 160/min

⚠️ Abnormal Findings:

🔹 Minimal or absent variability

🚨 Nursing Actions for Late Decels:

✅ Turn the client to her side

✅ Stop oxytocin if running

✅ Give IV fluids and oxygen as ordered

✅ Notify the provider

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

110 to 160 keeps the baby keen!

#252Pharmacology · post around 08:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #252!

💉 Can IV potassium ever be pushed?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Dilute It and Infuse with a Pump

🧠 Rationale: IV potassium is never given by IV push.

A fast dose can cause deadly dysrhythmias and cardiac arrest.

It must be diluted and run slowly on an infusion pump.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: IV Potassium Chloride

💊 Drug Class: Electrolyte replacement

❤️ Primary Use: Treating low potassium (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L)

⚠️ Watch For:

🔹 Burning or pain at the IV site

🔹 Peaked T waves if the level goes too high

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Always use an infusion pump

✅ Check kidney function and urine output first

✅ Keep the client on a cardiac monitor for higher rates

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Potassium: never push, always pump!

#253Endocrine · post around 10:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #253!

🧬 Low cortisol can change the color of the skin. Do you know how?

This is a HIGH-YIELD endocrine question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Bronze or Darkened Skin

🧠 Rationale: Addison disease is adrenal insufficiency: too little cortisol and aldosterone.

High ACTH levels darken the skin, giving a bronze look.

Moon face and weight gain point to Cushing syndrome instead.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Addison Disease

❤️ What Happens: The adrenal glands make too little cortisol and aldosterone

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Bronze skin

🔹 Weight loss and fatigue

🔹 Low sodium, high potassium, low glucose

🔹 Low blood pressure

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Teach lifelong steroid replacement

✅ Never stop steroids suddenly

✅ Extra doses may be needed during illness or stress

🚑 Emergency: Addisonian crisis causes severe low BP and shock. Expect IV fluids and IV hydrocortisone.

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Addison = Adding bronze to the skin, losing sodium and weight!

❤️ What vital sign do you ALWAYS check before a beta blocker?

This is a HIGH-YIELD cardiac question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.

.

.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Heart Rate 52 Beats per Minute

🧠 Rationale: Metoprolol is a beta blocker that lowers heart rate and blood pressure.

A heart rate below 60 usually means hold the dose and call the provider.

The other vital signs are within normal limits.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Metoprolol

💊 Drug Class: Beta blocker (the "olol" drugs)

❤️ Primary Use: High blood pressure, angina, heart failure, after a heart attack

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 Bradycardia

🔹 Low blood pressure and dizziness

🔹 Can hide signs of low blood sugar

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Check apical pulse and BP before every dose

✅ Teach slow position changes

✅ Never stop the drug suddenly

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

"Olol" drugs slow the heart: check the pulse before you give it!

🫁 One finding in the neck can signal a lung emergency. Do you know it?

This is a HIGH-YIELD respiratory question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Trachea Shifted Away from the Injured Side

🧠 Rationale: In tension pneumothorax, trapped air builds pressure in the chest.

That pressure pushes the trachea and heart toward the unaffected side.

This lowers cardiac output and can quickly cause shock.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Tension Pneumothorax

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Tracheal deviation

🔹 Absent breath sounds on the injured side

🔹 Severe shortness of breath

🔹 Low BP and fast heart rate

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Call the rapid response team

✅ Give high flow oxygen

✅ Prepare for needle decompression and a chest tube

🚑 Emergency: This can cause cardiac arrest within minutes.

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Tension pushes the trachea away from the trouble!

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ NPO to rest the pancreas

✅ IV fluids and pain control

✅ Monitor glucose and calcium

🚑 Watch For: Low calcium, shock and breathing problems

Lipase = Lights up the pancreas!

💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #258!

🩸 Chills and back pain during a transfusion. What comes FIRST?

This is a HIGH-YIELD safety question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Stop the Transfusion

🧠 Rationale: Chills, fever and low back pain suggest an acute transfusion reaction.

Stopping the blood right away limits how much enters the body.

Then keep the line open with normal saline and notify the provider and blood bank.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Blood Transfusion Reactions

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Chills and fever

🔹 Low back pain

🔹 Hives or itching

🔹 Shortness of breath or low BP

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Stop the transfusion

✅ Change the tubing and run normal saline

✅ Stay with the client and monitor vitals

✅ Send the blood bag back to the blood bank

⏱️ Key Fact: Most reactions happen in the first 15 minutes, so stay with the client

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Reaction? STOP the blood before anything else!

#245Pharmacology · post around 08:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #245!

💉 Can you mix insulin glargine with other insulins in the same syringe?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — It Should Not Be Mixed with Other Insulins

🧠 Rationale: Insulin glargine is a long-acting basal insulin.

Mixing it with other insulins can change how it is absorbed and how well it works.

It has no real peak and is given subcutaneously, never IV.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Insulin Glargine

💊 Drug Class: Long-acting insulin

❤️ Primary Use: Steady 24 hour basal blood glucose control

⚠️ Watch For:

🔹 Hypoglycemia: shaky, sweaty, confused

🔹 Injection site reactions

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Never mix in the same syringe

✅ Give once daily at the same time

✅ Give subcutaneously only

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Glargine goes it alone: no peak, no mixing, no IV!

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.

.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Call 911 if Pain Is Not Better 5 Minutes After One Dose

🧠 Rationale: Chest pain that does not improve 5 minutes after the first dose may be a heart attack.

Calling 911 early saves heart muscle.

The client may take 1 tablet every 5 minutes, up to 3 doses, as prescribed.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Sublingual Nitroglycerin

💊 Drug Class: Nitrate (vasodilator)

❤️ Primary Use: Relief of angina chest pain

⚠️ Side Effects:

🔹 Headache

🔹 Low blood pressure and dizziness

🔹 Flushing

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ Sit down before taking it

✅ Let it dissolve under the tongue

✅ Keep in the original dark glass bottle

✅ Avoid sildenafil and similar drugs

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

1 tab, 5 minutes, no relief? Call 911!

Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #247!

🧠 Pounding headache and sky-high BP in a spinal cord injury client. What is your FIRST move?

This is a HIGH-YIELD neuro question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Sit the Client Upright

🧠 Rationale: These are signs of autonomic dysreflexia, a medical emergency.

Sitting upright and lowering the legs helps lower blood pressure fast.

Next, find and remove the trigger. A full bladder is the most common cause.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Autonomic Dysreflexia

🧠 Who Is at Risk: Spinal cord injury at T6 or above

⚠️ Signs:

🔹 Severe hypertension

🔹 Pounding headache

🔹 Flushing and sweating above the injury

🔹 Slow heart rate

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Sit upright, lower the legs

✅ Loosen tight clothing

✅ Check bladder: catheter kinked or full?

✅ Check bowel for impaction

🚑 Escalate: Notify the provider. Antihypertensives may be needed if BP stays high.

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Sit up, then find the trigger: bladder, bowel, skin!

#248Respiratory · post around 15:00
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #248!

🫁 pH 7.30 and PaCO2 52. Can you interpret this ABG in 10 seconds?

This is a HIGH-YIELD ABG question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Respiratory Acidosis

🧠 Rationale: The pH is below 7.35, so this is acidosis.

The PaCO2 is high (above 45), which matches the acidosis, so the cause is respiratory.

The HCO3 is normal, so the kidneys have not compensated yet.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: ABG Interpretation

📊 Normal Values:

🔹 pH: 7.35 to 7.45

🔹 PaCO2: 35 to 45 mmHg

🔹 HCO3: 22 to 26 mEq/L

⚠️ Common Causes of Respiratory Acidosis:

🔹 COPD

🔹 Opioid or sedative oversedation

🔹 Hypoventilation

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Support breathing and airway

✅ Encourage cough and deep breathing

✅ Give oxygen as prescribed

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

ROME: Respiratory Opposite, Metabolic Equal!

💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #249!

🤰 Rh-negative mom, Rh-positive baby. What does the nurse give, and when?

This is a HIGH-YIELD maternity question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Give Rho(D) Immune Globulin Within 72 Hours

🧠 Rationale: The mother can make antibodies against Rh-positive blood.

Those antibodies could harm a future Rh-positive baby.

Rho(D) immune globulin given within 72 hours after birth helps prevent this.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Rh Incompatibility

💉 Medication: Rho(D) immune globulin (RhoGAM)

📅 When It Is Given:

🔹 Around 28 weeks of pregnancy

🔹 Within 72 hours after birth of an Rh-positive baby

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Give IM to the mother, not the baby

✅ Confirm the mother is Rh negative

✅ Check that consent is signed

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Rh negative mom gets RhoGAM: 28 weeks and 72 hours!

#238Pharmacology · post around 08:15
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #238!

🔥 Flushing and a red rash during a vancomycin infusion. What do you do FIRST?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: A — Stop the Infusion and Notify the Provider

🧠 Rationale: This is a vancomycin infusion reaction (often called red man syndrome or vancomycin flushing syndrome).

It is caused by histamine release when vancomycin is infused too fast.

Stop the infusion first, then notify the provider. The provider may order an antihistamine and restart the drug at a slower rate.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Vancomycin

💊 Drug Class: Glycopeptide antibiotic

🦠 Primary Use: Serious gram-positive infections including MRSA and C. difficile (oral)

⚠️ Watch For:

🔹 Flushing and rash of the face, neck and upper body

🔹 Ototoxicity (ringing in the ears, hearing loss)

🔹 Nephrotoxicity (rising creatinine, low urine output)

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Infuse slowly, usually over at least 60 minutes

✅ Monitor trough levels as ordered

✅ Monitor kidney function and hearing

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Vancomycin too fast = flushed face. Stop, notify, slow it down!

#239Electrolytes · post around 10:30
Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #239!

⚡ Potassium 6.8 and peaked T waves. What is your FIRST move?

This is a HIGH-YIELD electrolyte question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Place the Client on Continuous Cardiac Monitoring

🧠 Rationale: A normal potassium level is about 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L.

Severe hyperkalemia can cause dangerous dysrhythmias and cardiac arrest.

Peaked T waves show the heart is already affected, so continuous monitoring comes first while treatment is started.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Hyperkalemia

⚠️ Signs and Symptoms:

🔹 Peaked T waves and dysrhythmias

🔹 Muscle weakness

🔹 Paresthesias

🔹 Nausea and diarrhea

💉 Common Treatments:

✅ IV calcium gluconate to protect the heart

✅ IV regular insulin with dextrose to shift potassium into cells

✅ Sodium polystyrene sulfonate or other binders to remove potassium

✅ Dialysis for severe cases or kidney failure

🚨 Common Causes:

✅ Kidney failure

✅ Potassium-sparing diuretics and ACE inhibitors

✅ Tissue damage such as burns or crush injuries

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

High K = Heart at risk. Monitor first!

💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #240!

🧠 Expected side effect or lithium toxicity? Can you tell the difference?

This is a HIGH-YIELD mental health pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: C — Coarse Tremor and Persistent Vomiting

🧠 Rationale: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic range, usually about 0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L for maintenance.

A fine hand tremor, thirst and mild nausea are common expected effects.

A coarse tremor, persistent vomiting or diarrhea, and confusion point to toxicity. Hold the dose and notify the provider.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Lithium

💊 Drug Class: Mood stabilizer

🧠 Primary Use: Bipolar disorder

⚠️ Signs of Toxicity:

🔹 Coarse tremor

🔹 Persistent vomiting and diarrhea

🔹 Confusion and slurred speech

🔹 Muscle weakness and poor coordination

🚨 Patient Teaching:

✅ Drink 2 to 3 L of fluid daily

✅ Keep sodium intake steady. Low sodium raises lithium levels

✅ Avoid NSAIDs and get regular blood levels checked

✅ Report vomiting, diarrhea or heavy sweating since dehydration raises levels

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Fine tremor = fine. Coarse tremor = call!

Show caption
💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #241!

🧼 C. diff on your assignment. Which infection control step matters MOST?

This is a HIGH-YIELD infection control question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Wash Hands with Soap and Water

🧠 Rationale: C. difficile forms spores.

Alcohol-based hand rubs do not kill these spores.

Soap, water and friction physically remove the spores from your hands.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: C. difficile

🦠 What It Is: A spore-forming bacteria that causes severe diarrhea and colitis

⚠️ Risk Factors:

🔹 Recent antibiotic use

🔹 Older adults

🔹 Long hospital or nursing home stays

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Contact precautions with gown and gloves

✅ Soap and water hand hygiene

✅ Dedicated equipment such as a stethoscope for the room

✅ Clean the room with a bleach-based disinfectant

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

C. diff = spores. Spores beat sanitizer. Soap and water wins!

💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #242!

🩸 Heparin is running and the client is bleeding. Which antidote do you grab?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pharmacology question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Protamine Sulfate

🧠 Rationale: Protamine sulfate is the reversal agent for heparin.

Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not heparin.

Naloxone reverses opioids and flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Heparin

💊 Drug Class: Anticoagulant

❤️ Primary Use: Prevent and treat clots such as DVT and PE

🧪 Lab to Monitor: aPTT

⚠️ Watch For:

🔹 Bleeding gums, nosebleeds and blood in urine or stool

🔹 Bruising

🔹 Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (dropping platelets)

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Stop the infusion if bleeding occurs and notify the provider

✅ Use an infusion pump and double-check doses

✅ Use a soft toothbrush and electric razor

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Heparin = Protamine. Warfarin = Vitamin K!

💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #243!

🌬️ Why does pursed-lip breathing actually help clients with COPD?

This is a HIGH-YIELD respiratory question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — It Keeps Airways Open Longer During Exhalation

🧠 Rationale: In COPD, small airways collapse early during exhalation and trap air in the lungs.

Pursed-lip breathing creates back pressure that holds those airways open.

This helps the client push out more carbon dioxide and reduces shortness of breath.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: COPD Breathing

🫁 How to Teach It:

✅ Breathe in through the nose for about 2 counts

✅ Purse the lips like blowing out a candle

✅ Breathe out slowly for about 4 counts

⚠️ COPD Signs to Know:

🔹 Barrel chest

🔹 Use of accessory muscles

🔹 Chronic cough and sputum

🔹 Tripod positioning

🚨 Nursing Tips:

✅ High Fowler or tripod position helps breathing

✅ Give oxygen as prescribed and watch for CO2 retention

✅ Encourage small frequent meals to reduce fatigue

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Smell the roses, blow out the candle!

💊 NCLEX PRACTICE QUESTION #244!

🚨 Drooling, high fever and tripod position in a child. What should you NOT do?

This is a HIGH-YIELD pediatric question every nursing student should know! 🩺

👇 Comment your answer before checking!

.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.

✅ Correct Answer: B — Inspect the Throat with a Tongue Depressor

🧠 Rationale: Epiglottitis is a medical emergency because the swollen epiglottis can block the airway.

Putting anything in the throat can trigger a spasm and complete airway obstruction.

Keep the child calm, keep emergency airway equipment close and let the provider examine the throat in a controlled setting.

📚 NCLEX Must-Know: Epiglottitis

⚠️ The 4 Ds:

🔹 Drooling

🔹 Dysphagia (trouble swallowing)

🔹 Dysphonia (muffled voice)

🔹 Distressed breathing

🚨 Nursing Actions:

✅ Do NOT use a tongue depressor or throat swab

✅ Keep the child upright and calm, often on the parent's lap

✅ Have intubation and tracheostomy equipment at the bedside

✅ Avoid upsetting procedures that make the child cry

🛡️ Prevention: The Hib vaccine has made epiglottitis much less common

💡 NCLEX MEMORY TIP:

Drooling + tripod = Do NOT touch the throat!
